theory_concepts.title: A system is more than a set of parts
Reading the brief as an engineer

section_checks.section_title: A system is more than a set of parts

questions.prompt: Which description best explains an engineered system?
options: A group of parts stored together
Interacting components that transform inputs into outputs for a purpose
Any object made from more than one material
A product that works without people

feedback.message: A collection becomes a system only when the parts interact for a purpose.
Correct. The interactions and transformation are what make the components a system.
Using several materials does not by itself create a system; the components must interact.
People can operate, monitor or adjust a system, so independence from people is not required.

questions.help_prompt: Look for the choice that includes components, interaction, a transformation and a purpose.

questions.prompt: A box contains a lever arm, fasteners and elastic material. When would these parts become a system?
options: As soon as they are placed in the same box
When they are the same colour
When they are arranged to interact and perform a defined function
Only after the parts have been tested once

feedback.message: Being stored together does not create a functional relationship between the parts.
Appearance can support communication, but matching colour does not create a system.
Correct. The parts become a system when their interactions contribute to a shared purpose.
Testing can reveal system behaviour, but purposeful interactions are what make the parts a system.

questions.help_prompt: Ask whether the parts have defined relationships and a shared function.

questions.prompt: Which system boundary best supports an explanation of why a classroom Catapult frame shifted during a teacher-directed check?
options: Include only a list of loose materials and ignore how they interact
Place every person and object in the classroom inside one system boundary
Exclude the frame because it did not produce the intended movement
Place the designed components and their relationships inside the boundary, while identifying supervision and the controlled test setting as part of the wider situation

feedback.message: A list of materials does not show the component relationships that could explain the shift.
A boundary that includes the entire classroom is too broad to keep the system explanation focused.
The frame remains part of the system; its unwanted movement may be important evidence about an interaction.
Correct. This boundary keeps the engineered object focused while recognising the wider teacher-controlled situation.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit “A system is more than a set of parts” and ask what belongs to the designed object and what belongs to the wider test situation.

questions.prompt: A component is strong on its own but is positioned so it does not support the components that move. What is the best engineering conclusion?
options: Its individual strength guarantees that the whole system will be reliable
Component quality must be judged together with position, function and interaction in the whole system
Its colour should be changed before any other decision is made
The component should be ignored because only moving parts affect a system

feedback.message: A strong individual part can still contribute to weak system behaviour if its relationship to other parts is ineffective.
Correct. Engineers judge how a component works with the rest of the system, not its isolated quality alone.
Colour does not address the functional relationship described in the scenario.
Stationary components such as a frame can carry forces and strongly affect how moving parts behave.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the example of a strong component in the wrong position and focus on relationships, not isolated parts.

written_response.title: Explain a system relationship from evidence
written_response.prompt: During a teacher-directed stability check, the frame shifts when another component moves. Explain why this observation must be investigated as a system relationship rather than blamed on one part without evidence.

scaffold.label: Boundary
scaffold.prompt: State what you would place inside the designed-system boundary and what belongs to the wider teacher-controlled situation.

scaffold.label: Components
scaffold.prompt: Name two relevant types of component and explain how their functions could interact.

scaffold.label: Effect
scaffold.prompt: Explain how a change in one component or relationship could affect the whole system output.

scaffold.label: Evidence
scaffold.prompt: Identify an observation or comparison that could help test the explanation without prescribing a construction method.

success_cues: Defines a focused system boundary
Explains at least one component interaction
Connects a possible change to a whole-system effect
Uses teacher-directed evidence and avoids an unsupported cause claim

questions.prompt: In a system map, where should stored elastic energy be recorded before it is transferred?
options: Input
Process
Output
Feedback

feedback.message: Correct. Stored energy entering the transformation is an input to the system.
The process is the interaction that transfers or transforms the input.
The output is the resulting motion or other observable result after the transformation.
Feedback is information collected about the result and used for a decision.

questions.help_prompt: Identify what enters the transformation before any component moves.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of feedback in a Catapult design process?
options: It stores energy for later use
It records evidence so a designer can judge and adjust the system
It makes every component move faster
It replaces the need for a design brief

feedback.message: An energy store is a component; feedback is information about performance.
Correct. Feedback links observed results to a decision about keeping or changing the design.
Feedback can lead to many kinds of changes, not automatically greater speed.
The brief defines the problem; feedback helps judge how well a solution responds to it.

questions.help_prompt: Think about what information a result gives a designer.

questions.prompt: Repeated observations show that the Catapult results vary. When do those observations become useful feedback?
options: As soon as the numbers are copied, even if nobody considers them
When they are used to judge the result and guide a keep, investigate or controlled-change decision
Only when every repeated result is identical
When they replace the need to identify inputs and processes

feedback.message: Recorded observations are data, but feedback requires the information to inform a later decision.
Correct. Feedback closes the loop by connecting an observed output to the next reasoned decision.
Variation can itself be useful feedback; results do not need to be identical.
Feedback adds to a system map rather than replacing the need to explain inputs and processes.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the feedback paragraph and look for the step that turns an observed output into a next decision.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is the clearest input–process–output–feedback trace for a teacher-controlled Catapult observation?
options: Observed motion → stored energy → component interaction → ignore the result
Teacher feedback → material appears → every component moves identically → the brief is replaced
Stored energy → interactions transfer energy → observable motion and sound → observations guide the next decision
Sound → feedback stores energy → the process becomes a material → no decision is needed

feedback.message: This sequence begins with an output and does not use the result to guide a decision.
Feedback does not create material, guarantee identical motion or replace the authorised brief.
Correct. It follows the system from an input through a process and output, then returns evidence to the design decision.
Sound is an output, feedback is information, and a useful cycle must support a decision.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the input–process–output–feedback sequence and follow what enters, changes, appears, then informs a decision.

written_response.title: Turn an observation into feedback
written_response.prompt: A teacher-directed check produces movement, sound and visible frame shift, and the repeated results vary. Trace this situation through input, process, output and feedback, then justify one evidence-led next decision.

scaffold.label: Input
scaffold.prompt: Identify an energy or information input without inventing a launch setting.

scaffold.label: Process
scaffold.prompt: Explain how interacting components transfer or transform the input.

scaffold.label: Outputs
scaffold.prompt: Separate the intended observable result from sound, vibration, frame movement or variable test data.

scaffold.label: Feedback
scaffold.prompt: Explain how the observations could support a keep, investigate or one-controlled-change decision.

success_cues: Uses input, process, output and feedback accurately
Distinguishes observations from the decision they inform
Recognises more than one energy or motion output
Justifies a cautious next decision from evidence

section_checks.section_title: Reading the brief as an engineer

questions.prompt: Which statement from the brief is a constraint rather than a criterion?
options: The frame remains stable during a teacher-controlled test
The planned pine lengths total no more than the authorised 2400 mm
The parts stay aligned at a quality checkpoint
The result can be explained using test evidence

feedback.message: Stability describes an observable quality and can therefore be used as a criterion.
Correct. A fixed material allowance limits the design and is therefore a constraint.
Alignment describes an observable quality rather than a resource limit.
Using evidence is an observable expectation rather than a limit on the design.

questions.help_prompt: A constraint limits what the designer may use or do; a criterion describes what success should look like.

questions.prompt: What should a student do when the booklet's ‘10mm² Pine’ wording is unclear?
options: Choose a likely cross-section and continue
Copy a dimension from another Catapult website
Ask the teacher to confirm the intended stock before relying on it
Ignore all material limits

feedback.message: Guessing could create a practical error because the notation is genuinely ambiguous.
Another course is not authority for this project's material specification.
Correct. A teacher confirmation preserves the source boundary and prevents an unsafe or wasteful assumption.
The confirmed 2400 mm planned-length limit still applies even though the cross-section is unclear.

questions.help_prompt: Separate the confirmed timber allowance from the unresolved stock cross-section.

questions.prompt: Which wording is the strongest provisional criterion to take to the teacher for confirmation?
options: The Catapult is good
The Catapult looks powerful
The frame remains in its marked start position throughout a teacher-controlled stability check
The design uses as much pine as possible

feedback.message: “Good” is too vague because it does not identify an observable feature or evidence.
Appearance and the word “powerful” do not establish a testable measure of success.
Correct. This provisional wording states an observable success condition while leaving approval and test conditions with the teacher.
Using more material is not automatically a sign of quality and must remain within the authorised limit.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the distinction between a method for comparing results and a criterion that states an observable success condition.

questions.prompt: A concept stays within the confirmed material constraints, but its only success claim is “it should work well”. What should the designer do next?
options: Treat meeting the constraints as proof that the design will succeed
Add an unsupported dimension so the claim sounds precise
Ignore criteria until after all practical work is complete
Replace the vague claim with an observable provisional criterion and identify evidence for teacher confirmation

feedback.message: Meeting constraints keeps a design within boundaries but does not prove its quality or performance.
An invented dimension is not authorised evidence and does not resolve the vague claim.
Criteria are needed before testing so the evidence can answer a clear question.
Correct. A testable provisional criterion links the success claim to evidence and can then be confirmed by the teacher.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit why constraints and criteria do different jobs: one limits the solution and the other describes evidence of success.

written_response.title: Audit a brief statement
written_response.prompt: A concept uses only the authorised material types and plans less than 2400 mm of pine, but the designer says it will be “strong and accurate”. Explain what the brief evidence establishes, what remains vague, and what must be confirmed before the claim can guide testing.

scaffold.label: Constraints
scaffold.prompt: Identify the confirmed boundaries in the scenario and explain what meeting them does and does not prove.

scaffold.label: Criterion
scaffold.prompt: Rewrite one vague word as a provisional observable criterion without inventing a formal project requirement.

scaffold.label: Evidence
scaffold.prompt: Name the type of observation or measurement that could support the provisional criterion.

scaffold.label: Confirm
scaffold.prompt: State which criterion and test conditions remain teacher controlled and why the designer should pause.

success_cues: Distinguishes constraints from criteria
Uses the authorised 2400 mm limit accurately
Turns vague wording into an evidence-linked provisional criterion
Clearly identifies the teacher-confirmation boundary

capstone.title: Turn the brief into a system plan
capstone.prompt: Explain how a student-designed Catapult can be treated as an engineered system while staying inside the authorised brief.

scaffold.label: Map
scaffold.prompt: Name one input, one process and one output without prescribing a construction method.

scaffold.label: Connect
scaffold.prompt: Explain how two possible components would need to interact for the system to work.

scaffold.label: Bound
scaffold.prompt: State one confirmed constraint and one useful, testable criterion.

scaffold.label: Improve
scaffold.prompt: Describe what feedback could be collected and how it could support one design decision.

success_cues: Uses input–process–output–feedback accurately
Distinguishes a criterion from a constraint
Uses the confirmed 2400 mm planned-pine limit without inventing dimensions
Explains a component interaction and a reasoned improvement

applied_learning_activity.title: System map stress test
applied_learning_activity.purpose: Practise turning a design brief into a system map and checking whether each component has a purpose.
applied_learning_activity.lesson_placement: After criteria and constraints, before the module capstone
ordered_steps: Type the authorised need and confirmed constraints in separate fields.
Sort six teacher-provided example statements into input, process, output or feedback.
Choose one possible component and explain what it would interact with.
Rewrite one vague success statement as an observable criterion.
Review the map and remove any claim that is not authorised by the brief.
applied_learning_activity.evidence_to_save: Completed system map plus the rewritten criterion, saved as formative practice.
applied_learning_activity.extension: Add a second feedback source and explain which design decision it could change.
applied_learning_activity.support: Use the sentence frame: ‘The system takes ___ as an input, ___ changes or transfers it, and the output is ___.’
applied_learning_activity.printable_option: Four-column input–process–output–feedback table with a criteria/constraints box.

folio_connection.prompt: Use your checked brief map to write the need, authorised constraints and provisional testable criteria in your own words.
folio_connection.relationship: The activity rehearses the ideas; the folio keeps only the student's selected brief evidence.

questions.prompt: Which response best shows a planned approach to workshop safety?
options: Start quickly and copy what another student does
Identify the hazard, follow teacher-approved controls and stop to ask when unsure
Use any familiar tool without checking permission
Rely on carefulness instead of a control

feedback.message: Another student's action is not a substitute for the teacher's approved procedure.
Correct. Hazard recognition, approved controls and stop/ask decisions work together as a safety system.
Familiarity does not establish permission, readiness or the correct process for this class.
Care matters, but it does not replace a specific, teacher-approved control.

questions.help_prompt: Look for the choice that joins hazard recognition, an authorised control and a decision point.

questions.prompt: A student's planned process does not match the teacher demonstration. What is the safest next step?
options: Continue because the plan is already written
Ask a classmate to decide
Stop and ask the teacher before proceeding
Change the process silently

feedback.message: A written plan does not override a teacher demonstration or local control.
A classmate cannot authorise a local workshop procedure.
Correct. Stop and ask protects the student and allows the plan to be corrected before work resumes.
An unrecorded change can introduce a new risk and breaks the planned safety system.

questions.help_prompt: When the source of authority and the written plan disagree, pause before taking practical action.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a hazard from risk?
options: A hazard has the potential to cause harm, while risk considers likelihood and possible seriousness in the actual context
A hazard is the chance of harm, while risk is the name of a tool
A hazard disappears after an online module is completed
Risk is identical in every workshop situation

feedback.message: Correct. Risk depends on the hazard, task, condition, people and controls in the particular situation.
A hazard is the source or situation with potential for harm; risk considers likelihood and seriousness.
Training can support readiness, but it does not remove a hazard or replace current controls.
Risk changes with the task, condition and controls, so it cannot be assumed to be identical everywhere.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the opening safety paragraph and compare “potential to cause harm” with “likelihood and seriousness in context”.

questions.prompt: A student has completed the required online safety learning, but the work area or instruction has changed. What does safe readiness require?
options: Stop, reassess the current situation and follow the teacher-approved control before proceeding
Continue because online completion gives permanent permission for every situation
Ask another student to approve the changed condition
Ignore the change if the planned task is familiar

feedback.message: Correct. Readiness includes responding to changed conditions and using the current teacher-approved control.
Online learning is one part of readiness; it does not give blanket permission or replace current checks.
Another student cannot authorise a local workshop procedure or control.
Familiarity does not remove the need to respond when the work area or instruction changes.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the stop–think–check–ask decision and remember that current conditions still matter after training.

written_response.title: Justify a safe stop-and-ask decision
written_response.prompt: Before a teacher-approved practical task begins, a student notices that one instruction is unclear and that the work area is not in the condition they expected. Explain why pausing is part of a planned safety system rather than a failure to be ready.

scaffold.label: Hazard
scaffold.prompt: Identify the potential for harm without inventing a specific workshop rule.

scaffold.label: Risk
scaffold.prompt: Explain how the task, condition, people and existing controls affect likelihood and possible seriousness.

scaffold.label: Decision
scaffold.prompt: Justify stopping before practical action and state what needs clarification.

scaffold.label: Authority
scaffold.prompt: Explain why teacher demonstration, permission and the local procedure control what happens next.

success_cues: Distinguishes hazard from contextual risk
Explains a stop-and-ask decision
Recognises that conditions and controls can change
Leaves local procedures and permission teacher controlled

questions.prompt: Which tool group is mainly used to keep a workpiece from moving during a teacher-approved process?
options: Measuring and marking
Holding
Shaping
Joining

feedback.message: Measuring and marking tools establish size or position; they do not mainly secure the workpiece.
Correct. Holding tools support control by keeping the workpiece secure as directed.
Shaping tools change a surface or form rather than mainly securing it.
Joining tools or processes connect parts; holding is the category focused on preventing movement.

questions.help_prompt: Focus on the purpose of the tool group, not the name of a particular workshop tool.

questions.prompt: What must be checked before a tool shown in the source booklet is used?
options: Whether it appears in another school's project
Whether the student likes using it
Whether the teacher has approved it and taught the local procedure
Whether it can finish the task fastest

feedback.message: Another school's practice does not establish local permission or procedure.
Preference does not establish suitability, readiness or approval.
Correct. The picture identifies a learning prompt, not permission or an operating procedure.
Speed is secondary to suitability and teacher-approved use.

questions.help_prompt: A source image can support identification, but local access and use remain teacher-controlled.

questions.prompt: Two teacher-approved tools can perform the same broad function. Which comparison best supports selection?
options: Choose the tool that looks most powerful
Choose the tool used by the greatest number of classmates
Compare material suitability, required accuracy, access, finish and the approved process
Assume tools in the same category always produce the same result

feedback.message: Powerful appearance does not establish suitability, accuracy, access or finish.
Popularity does not show that a tool suits this material, function or approved process.
Correct. Tool selection connects the required function to the material, quality evidence and teacher-approved process.
Tools in the same category can suit different situations and leave different results.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the selection factors listed after the tool-function categories, then connect them to the required result.

questions.prompt: After a teacher-approved measuring and marking stage, which evidence best shows that the work is ready for the next planned process?
options: The student finished before everyone else
The mark is clear, agrees with the drawing and has been checked
A different process has already started
The tool was familiar to the student

feedback.message: Speed does not show that the mark is accurate or consistent with the design information.
Correct. Readiness evidence should show that the communicated position is clear, consistent and checked before work continues.
Starting the next process before the checkpoint removes the chance to correct the information safely.
Familiarity does not prove that the result meets the planned requirement.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the worked example and look for the checkpoint that connects the mark to the drawing before another process begins.

written_response.title: Select by function and evidence
written_response.prompt: A planned component needs a position communicated clearly before later work can begin. Explain how a student should move from the required function to a teacher-approved tool decision and a meaningful readiness checkpoint.

scaffold.label: Function
scaffold.prompt: State the immediate function and explain why it comes before choosing a named tool.

scaffold.label: Compare
scaffold.prompt: Describe how material, accuracy, access and finish could affect selection between approved options.

scaffold.label: Approve
scaffold.prompt: Identify where teacher permission and the local operating procedure enter the decision.

scaffold.label: Checkpoint
scaffold.prompt: Explain what observable evidence would show the result is ready for the next stage.

success_cues: Begins with the required function
Uses relevant selection factors rather than familiarity or speed
Preserves the teacher-controlled operating boundary
Defines a clear evidence-based checkpoint

questions.prompt: Why should a designer inspect pine rather than assume every piece behaves identically?
options: Pine always changes colour during use
Grain direction, knots and natural variation can affect its behaviour
All pine is too flexible for prototypes
Inspection confirms the missing stock cross-section

feedback.message: Colour change is not the main reason for checking structural behaviour.
Correct. Timber is a natural material, so visible features and grain can influence performance and workability.
Pine can be suitable for classroom prototypes; its suitability depends on the actual piece and purpose.
Inspection cannot resolve the source's ambiguous stock notation; that needs teacher confirmation.

questions.help_prompt: Think about timber as a natural material with features that vary from piece to piece.

questions.prompt: What does elastic deformation mean?
options: The material changes shape and returns when the force is removed, within its elastic range
The material changes permanently after every force
The material cannot store energy
The material becomes stronger each time it is stretched

feedback.message: Correct. Reversible shape change within the elastic range distinguishes elastic from permanent deformation.
A permanent change is plastic or permanent deformation, not elastic deformation.
Elastic materials can store energy while deformed, although not all stored energy becomes useful output.
Repeated stretching can damage or change a material; it does not automatically make it stronger.

questions.help_prompt: Ask what happens to the material after the force is removed.

questions.prompt: After a force is removed, one sample returns towards its earlier shape while another remains changed. Which explanation is correct?
options: The returning sample shows elastic behaviour, while the lasting change is permanent deformation
Both samples show identical elastic deformation
The lasting change proves the sample is storing more useful energy
Neither observation provides information about material behaviour

feedback.message: Correct. Returning towards the earlier shape indicates elastic behaviour; a change that remains is permanent deformation.
A lasting shape change differs from deformation that reverses after the force is removed.
Permanent change can indicate damage or use beyond a suitable range; it does not prove more useful stored energy.
The response after force removal is direct evidence about elastic or permanent behaviour.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the definitions of elastic and permanent deformation and focus on what remains after the force is removed.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports a decision about whether an actual piece of pine suits a planned function?
options: Inspect its grain, knots and condition, then connect those observations to function and the approved process
Assume it behaves exactly like every other piece labelled pine
Judge only its colour
Use the unresolved booklet cross-section as if it were confirmed

feedback.message: Correct. Material observations become useful when they are connected to function and a teacher-approved process.
Timber is naturally variable, so a category label cannot replace inspection of the actual piece.
Colour alone does not establish workability, condition or functional suitability.
The ambiguous stock notation remains a teacher-confirmation issue and must not be treated as settled.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the pine paragraph and connect natural variation in the actual piece to its required function.

written_response.title: Interpret material behaviour without overclaiming
written_response.prompt: Before practical work, one pine piece has a visible knot and a material sample in a teacher-controlled demonstration does not fully return after the force is removed. Explain what these observations suggest, what they do not prove, and what should be confirmed next.

scaffold.label: Timber
scaffold.prompt: Explain how grain, knots and natural variation can make inspection of the actual pine piece important.

scaffold.label: Elasticity
scaffold.prompt: Distinguish elastic behaviour from a permanent change after the force is removed.

scaffold.label: Limits
scaffold.prompt: Explain why an observation does not authorise a student to set an elastic arrangement or operating limit.

scaffold.label: Decision
scaffold.prompt: State what material suitability, stock information or practical condition must be confirmed by the teacher.

success_cues: Uses timber-variation evidence accurately
Distinguishes elastic from permanent deformation
Avoids claiming that one observation proves complete suitability
Preserves teacher control of material and operating decisions

capstone.title: Make a source-safe workshop decision
capstone.prompt: A student needs to prepare one timber component, but the exact local process has not been supplied on the website. Explain how the student should make a safe, evidence-based preparation decision.

scaffold.label: Function
scaffold.prompt: State what the component needs to do and one relevant material property.

scaffold.label: Tool group
scaffold.prompt: Name the types of tool functions that may be needed, without naming an unapproved procedure.

scaffold.label: Safety system
scaffold.prompt: Identify what must be confirmed by the teacher before practical work begins.

scaffold.label: Decision
scaffold.prompt: Justify a stop/ask or proceed decision using the available evidence.

success_cues: Links material properties to function
Uses tool groups rather than inventing an operating sequence
Keeps permission, OnGuard and local controls teacher-controlled
Explains why the decision reduces uncertainty

modules.title: Siege Engines, Levers and the Woomera

theory_concepts.title: A woomera in its own cultural and technological context

questions.prompt: Which comparison correctly distinguishes historical siege-engine systems?
options: Every system stores energy in the same way
A trebuchet can use gravitational potential energy, while other systems may use tension or torsion
Only modern systems transform energy
The energy store decides the historical date by itself

feedback.message: Historical systems used different arrangements and energy stores to perform related functions.
Correct. Comparing the energy store and component interactions reveals important system differences.
Energy transformation is not unique to modern technology.
An energy store is one technical feature; dating requires reliable historical evidence.

questions.help_prompt: Compare how energy is stored before the main movement begins.

questions.prompt: Why is an onager, ballista and trebuchet comparison stronger when it includes components as well as names?
options: Component interactions explain how each system performs its function
A longer component list automatically explains the system more clearly
Components prove that all three work identically
Names are not part of historical research

feedback.message: Correct. Components and their interactions reveal the system's energy transfer and control.
A list without relationships does not explain how the system performs its function.
The point of comparison is to find meaningful similarities and differences, not to prove identity.
Accurate names matter, but names alone do not explain how a system works.

questions.help_prompt: Ask what information explains function rather than merely identifying the object.

questions.prompt: Why is the reset stage useful when comparing two historical projectile systems?
options: It proves that the larger system is always more advanced
It removes the need to identify the energy store
It shows how the energy store must be restored and reveals demands created by the component arrangement
It gives a complete account of the system’s cultural history by itself

feedback.message: Size does not establish superiority, and system comparisons should not create a ranking.
Resetting can be explained only by first understanding where and how energy is stored.
Correct. Resetting connects the energy store, moving components and practical trade-offs in the system.
A technical reset relationship is not a complete historical or cultural account.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the system-comparison questions and include what must be reset after the output occurs.

questions.prompt: Two historical systems produce a similar broad output. Which evidence is needed before claiming that they work in the same way?
options: Only their names
Only the shape of the projectile
A statement that one design is better
Their energy stores, moving components, frame relationships and reset demands

feedback.message: Names identify systems but do not explain their internal energy transfer or component relationships.
A projectile shape alone cannot show how the whole system stores and transfers energy.
A ranking is not evidence about how either system works.
Correct. This evidence supports a system-level comparison rather than an assumption based on output alone.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit “Different systems, different energy stores” and compare the internal relationships, not just the visible output.

It can fully explain every form, name, use and cultural meaning
It proves the technology has the same purpose as a siege engine
It cannot show any relationship between arm extension, force and speed

A shared lever principle does not make the technologies or their purposes equivalent.

theory_concepts.title: Newton's three laws in one system

questions.prompt: Which statement best follows conservation of energy in a Catapult system?
options: Useful energy is created when the lever moves
Stored energy is transferred and transformed, with some spreading to sound, heat, vibration and air movement
All stored energy becomes useful motion
Energy disappears when a component stops

feedback.message: The system transforms existing energy; it does not create energy from nothing.
Correct. Total energy is conserved even though it spreads into less useful forms.
Real systems transfer some energy to sound, heat, vibration and the surroundings.
Energy is transferred or transformed rather than disappearing.

questions.help_prompt: Track every energy destination, including transfers that are not part of the intended output.

questions.prompt: Why is a loud sound during movement evidence about the energy chain?
options: It shows that some energy has transferred to sound
It proves the system is more accurate
It means energy conservation has failed
It identifies the correct local test procedure

feedback.message: Correct. Sound is one destination for energy that is not part of the intended motion output.
Sound alone gives no reliable evidence about accuracy.
Energy spreading to sound is consistent with conservation of energy.
An observation does not establish the teacher-controlled test procedure.

questions.help_prompt: Consider whether the sound is a form of transferred energy rather than the intended output.

questions.prompt: Which statement uses force and energy language accurately?
options: A component contains force until it creates energy
Work can store elastic potential energy, and forces between objects can change motion as energy is transferred
Sound destroys the energy that the system no longer needs
The frame produces new energy whenever it moves

feedback.message: Force is an interaction, not a substance stored inside a component, and energy is not created from nothing.
Correct. This separates stored energy from forces that act during interactions and transfers.
Sound is an energy transfer to the surroundings, not evidence that energy has been destroyed.
Unwanted frame motion receives energy from the system; it does not create new energy.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the opening energy paragraph and separate stored elastic potential energy from force as an interaction.

questions.prompt: During a teacher-controlled observation, the frame moves as well as the intended moving component. What does the frame motion suggest?
options: Energy conservation has stopped applying
Some energy is following an unintended pathway through the system
The frame has become the input material
The intended output must be perfectly consistent

feedback.message: Energy is still conserved; the observation shows where some of it is being transferred.
Correct. Unwanted frame motion is an observable energy destination that may help explain inconsistent performance.
The frame is a system component, not an input material in this energy-chain description.
Unwanted frame motion may contribute to variation rather than proving perfect consistency.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the list of sound, heat, vibration, air movement and unwanted frame motion as energy-transfer pathways.

written_response.prompt: A teacher-controlled observation shows intended motion together with a loud sound, vibration and visible frame movement. Explain how conservation of energy applies and why these observations matter when investigating inconsistent performance.

scaffold.prompt: Identify how work can create an elastic potential energy store without saying that a component contains force.

scaffold.prompt: Trace energy into moving components and the intended observable output.

scaffold.prompt: Explain how sound, vibration and frame motion are energy transfers rather than disappearing energy.

scaffold.prompt: Use the observations to identify one pathway worth investigating through teacher-directed evidence.

Distinguishes energy from force

section_checks.section_title: Newton's three laws in one system

questions.prompt: Which observation best illustrates Newton's first law?
options: An object remains at rest until an unbalanced force acts
A larger net force always creates less acceleration
Action and reaction act on the same object
Mass has no effect on motion

feedback.message: Correct. A change in motion requires a net external force.
For the same mass, a larger net force produces greater acceleration, not less.
A third-law pair acts on two different interacting objects.
Mass is part of the relationship between net force and acceleration.

questions.help_prompt: Look for the statement about motion staying unchanged until a net force acts.

questions.prompt: Why do an action force and its reaction force not cancel each other?
options: One force happens much later
They are unequal
They act on different interacting objects
Only the action force is real

feedback.message: A third-law pair occurs at the same time during the interaction.
The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
Correct. Because the pair acts on different objects, it does not cancel on a single free-body view.
Both forces in the interaction are real.

questions.help_prompt: Identify the two objects and assign one force to each object.

questions.prompt: For the same object mass, what happens to acceleration when the net force becomes larger?
options: Acceleration becomes smaller
Acceleration becomes larger
Acceleration must remain zero
Mass disappears from the relationship

feedback.message: For the same mass, a smaller rather than larger net force would produce the smaller acceleration.
Correct. Newton’s second law links a larger net force to a larger acceleration when mass stays the same.
A non-zero net force changes motion, so acceleration does not have to remain zero.
Mass remains part of the force–mass–acceleration relationship even when it is held constant.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit Newton’s second law and hold mass constant while comparing the size of the net force.

questions.prompt: Why should an engineer draw separate force diagrams for two interacting objects?
options: To show that only one object experiences a real force
To make equal-and-opposite forces unequal
To remove gravity and air resistance from every analysis
To assign each force to the object it acts on and avoid treating a third-law pair as if it cancels on one object

feedback.message: Both objects in an interaction experience real forces.
Drawing the forces separately does not change their equal-and-opposite relationship.
Relevant external forces still need to be considered for the object being analysed.
Correct. Separate diagrams clarify which forces combine on each object and which forces form an interaction pair across objects.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the final Newton’s-law paragraph and identify which object receives each force.

written_response.title: Use all three laws in one interaction

scaffold.prompt: Name the two interacting objects and describe the equal-and-opposite force pair acting on different objects.

scaffold.prompt: Explain what separate force diagrams would clarify about each object’s motion.

success_cues: Applies each Newton’s law to the stated interaction
Uses net force and acceleration accurately

Explains the value of object-specific force diagrams

questions.prompt: What makes a prototype investigation a fair comparison?
options: Changing several features at once
Changing one planned variable while keeping relevant conditions consistent
Keeping only the best result
Using a different measure in every trial

feedback.message: Several simultaneous changes make it difficult to identify the cause of a result.
Correct. A single planned change and consistent conditions support a defensible comparison.
Selecting only the best result hides variation and weakens the evidence.
Consistent measures are needed if results are to be compared.

questions.help_prompt: Ask what must stay the same so the effect of one change can be judged.

questions.prompt: Why should a teacher-directed prototype test be repeated?
options: To make every result identical
To reveal consistency, variation and possible anomalies
To avoid recording controlled variables
To make the most extreme result more believable

feedback.message: Repeated results commonly vary; the purpose is to understand that variation.
Correct. Repeats show whether a pattern is dependable and help identify unusual results.
Controlled variables still need to be recorded for a fair comparison.
Repeats show the whole pattern; they do not give special authority to the most extreme result.

questions.help_prompt: Think about what a set of results reveals that one result cannot.

questions.prompt: What makes an unfinished prototype useful evidence?
options: It investigates a clear relationship and reduces uncertainty before full production
It looks exactly like the finished product
It changes several features so more happens in one trial
It guarantees that the final design cannot fail

feedback.message: Correct. Its value comes from a clear investigation and evidence that informs later decisions.
A prototype can be useful without a finished appearance if it answers a focused question.
Changing several features weakens the ability to connect a result to one cause.
Prototype evidence reduces uncertainty; it does not guarantee a perfect final design.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit why prototype value comes from the question and evidence rather than finished appearance.

questions.prompt: Which prototype record gives another person the strongest basis for checking the conclusion?
options: Only the best result and a claim that the change worked
A photograph with no labels or explanation
A list of several simultaneous changes with no baseline
The question, changed variable, controlled variables, repeated observations, anomalies and evidence-led conclusion

feedback.message: Selecting only the best result hides variation and does not show how the conclusion was reached.
A photograph can support evidence, but without context it does not explain the question or conclusion.
Several untracked changes make it difficult to identify what caused the result.
Correct. This record makes the method, pattern, uncertainty and decision visible for review.

theory_concepts.title: Drawings that agree with each other

questions.prompt: Why should a designer generate genuinely different ideas before selecting one?
options: It creates alternatives that can be compared against the brief
It guarantees the first idea will be chosen
It removes the need for research
It makes every idea equally suitable

feedback.message: Correct. Different alternatives make comparison and reasoned selection possible.
The first idea may be useful, but selection should follow comparison rather than habit.
Research can still inform how ideas respond to materials, systems and constraints.
Ideas will have different strengths, risks and fit with the brief.

questions.help_prompt: Think about what evidence a designer needs before committing resources to one option.

questions.prompt: What makes a PMI comparison useful for design selection?
options: It records only positive features
It links pluses, minuses and interesting questions to the brief and evidence
It replaces the final justification
It uses appearance as the only deciding factor

feedback.message: A balanced comparison must also consider limitations and unresolved questions.
Correct. The PMI becomes useful when each observation helps judge suitability.
The PMI informs selection; the designer must still explain the final decision.
Appearance can matter, but system function, material limits and other brief needs also matter.

questions.prompt: Which pair represents genuinely divergent design ideas?
options: The same component arrangement shown in two colours
The same sketch copied with a different title
Concepts that organise component relationships or manage stability in meaningfully different ways
One concept drawn neatly and the same concept drawn quickly

feedback.message: Changing colour does not create a different system idea.
A new title does not change the concept’s component relationships.
Correct. Divergent ideas explore meaningful alternatives that can be compared against the brief.
Drawing quality changes presentation, not the underlying design concept.

Choose the concept with the most decorative detail
Choose either concept because meeting constraints makes all alternatives equally suitable

feedback.message: Preference alone does not show why the concept is the strongest response to the brief.
Decoration may matter, but it cannot replace evidence about the system and confirmed needs.
Constraints define boundaries; concepts can still differ in likely performance, production demands and evidence.
Correct. A strong justification uses brief evidence, recognises a trade-off and identifies uncertainty.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of aligned front, top and side orthographic views?
options: To show the object from consistent directions without perspective distortion
To make the page decorative
To avoid showing dimensions
To replace every written production decision

feedback.message: Correct. Related views communicate shape and position clearly from standard directions.
Technical views exist to communicate, not merely decorate.
Dimensions and part labels often make the views more useful for planning.
Drawings support production planning but do not capture every decision or teacher approval.

questions.prompt: A part is labelled with different lengths in the side view and cutting list. What should happen next?
options: Use whichever number is larger
Ignore the drawing and start production
Resolve the inconsistency and obtain teacher approval before relying on the plan
Average the two lengths

feedback.message: Choosing the larger number does not establish which record is correct.
An inconsistent plan should not guide practical work.

A different colour for every line
Permission to ignore contradictions between records

Correct. Production information depends on views, labels and dimensions that agree, not visual appeal alone.
Line colour does not replace consistent technical information.
Contradictions must be resolved before the records guide practical work.

The top view omits a feature shown elsewhere
The page contains realistic shadows
Corresponding features align in the related views and repeated labels and dimensions agree

feedback.message: Unexplained scale changes create ambiguity rather than demonstrating agreement.
An omitted corresponding feature suggests the design is not fully communicated.
Realistic shadows may help appearance but are not evidence that technical views agree.
Correct. Alignment and consistent repeated information show that the views communicate one design.

questions.prompt: How is the planned total length for one cutting-list row calculated?
options: Multiply the planned length of one part by its quantity
Add the part name to the material name
Subtract every row from 2400 mm before checking quantity
Use the largest dimension shown anywhere in the drawing

feedback.message: Correct. Each row total is planned length per part multiplied by the number of those parts.
Names identify the item but do not calculate its material total.
The row total must be calculated before all rows can be compared with the overall limit.
The calculation must use the planned length and quantity for that specific listed part.

questions.prompt: Which cross-check is most likely to reveal a missing or unsupported item in a cutting list?
options: Choose the row with the longest part and ignore the others
Trace every listed part back to a labelled design view and check that every required drawn part appears in the list
Round every total to 2400 mm
Assume a correct grand total proves every row is complete

feedback.message: Ignoring other rows prevents a complete material and design check.
Correct. Two-way tracing between the drawings and list can reveal omissions, duplicates or unsupported items.
The authorised limit is a maximum, not a number to which every plan should be rounded.
Arithmetic can be correct even when a part is missing or does not match the design.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit how the cutting list links the drawing to material planning and check the link in both directions.

questions.prompt: What is a dependency in a production plan?
options: A task that must be completed or checked before a later task can proceed
A decorative detail added at the end
A task that can be completed at any time without affecting later work
Any two tasks completed by different students

feedback.message: Correct. Dependencies help place work and checkpoints in a logical order.
A decoration is not necessarily connected to the order of later work.
If the timing cannot affect later work, the task does not create a dependency.
Different people can complete tasks, but a dependency exists only when one task relies on another.

questions.help_prompt: Ask whether a later task would be unreliable or impossible until the earlier one is complete.

questions.prompt: Why should a production sequence include teacher-approved checkpoints?
options: To detect errors before later work makes them harder to correct
To create a universal Catapult recipe
To remove the need for measurements
To prove practical competence automatically

feedback.message: Correct. A well-placed checkpoint protects materials, time and alignment before the next dependency.
The student's sequence remains design-specific and teacher-approved; it is not a universal recipe.
Measurements and visual checks are often part of a checkpoint.
A website record cannot replace teacher observation or certify competence.

questions.help_prompt: Think about the cost of discovering a problem only after several dependent tasks are complete.

questions.prompt: Which situation most clearly shows a production dependency?
options: A caption colour is chosen after the report is finished
A later component can only be checked for fit after the supporting frame has been aligned
Two unrelated notes are typed on different days
A student prefers one task to another

feedback.message: A visual choice in the report does not make one production task rely on another.
Correct. The later fit check relies on the supporting frame being positioned and checked first.
Timing alone does not create a dependency when neither task relies on the other.
Preference does not show that one production task requires an earlier task or check.

questions.help_prompt: Ask whether the later task could be judged reliably before the earlier work was completed and checked.

questions.prompt: At a planned checkpoint, the work does not match the approved design information. What is the strongest next decision?
options: Begin the dependent task and hope the mismatch disappears
Change several features so at least one may help
Delete the checkpoint record so the folio looks successful
Stop before the dependent task, record the mismatch and follow the teacher-approved response

feedback.message: Continuing can make the mismatch harder to correct and can affect dependent work.
Several changes hide which response affected the result and may move beyond the approved process.
Honest evidence includes problems and decisions; removing it weakens the production record.
Correct. The checkpoint exists to protect later work by making the mismatch and approved response visible.

questions.help_prompt: Return to the paragraph explaining why checkpoints are planned before dependent work begins.

written_response.title: Use a checkpoint to protect later work
written_response.prompt: A later component depends on the base and frame being aligned, but a planned teacher-approved checkpoint reveals a mismatch. Explain why the sequence should pause and justify what evidence and decision are needed before the dependent task begins.

scaffold.label: Dependency
scaffold.prompt: Start with: “The later task depends on ___ because ___.”

scaffold.label: Checkpoint evidence
scaffold.prompt: Identify the approved design information and observable comparison that would show the mismatch.

scaffold.label: Decision
scaffold.prompt: Explain why stopping now protects time, material and later alignment.

scaffold.label: Next step
scaffold.prompt: State what must be recorded and confirmed by the teacher before production continues.

success_cues: Explains a genuine task dependency
Uses observable evidence rather than preference
Keeps the practical response teacher-approved
Connects the checkpoint to the quality of later work

section_checks.section_title: Structures carry forces through load paths

questions.prompt: What is a load path?
options: The route forces take through connected structural parts to the supports
The walking route through the workshop
A list of project materials
The order of theory modules

feedback.message: Correct. Load-path thinking connects forces, members, joints and supports.
Workshop movement matters for local safety, but it is not the structural meaning of load path.
A material list identifies resources rather than the transfer of forces.
Module order is a learning sequence, not a structural force route.

questions.help_prompt: Trace where a force enters a structure and how it reaches the supporting surface.

questions.prompt: Why can triangular bracing increase the rigidity of a frame?
options: A triangle resists changing shape unless a member or joint changes length or fails
It removes every force from the frame
It guarantees all joints are strong
It makes material properties irrelevant

feedback.message: Correct. Triangulation can direct loads through members while resisting easy shape change.
Bracing redirects and carries forces; it does not make forces disappear.
Weak, misaligned or unsuitable joints can still reduce structural quality.
Member and joint materials still affect stiffness, strength and behaviour.

questions.help_prompt: Compare how easily a rectangle and a triangle can change shape at their corners.

questions.prompt: Which description identifies compression in a structural member?
options: Forces twist the member around an axis
Forces pull the member
Nearby sections are encouraged to slide past each other
Forces squeeze the member

feedback.message: Twisting around an axis describes torsion.
Pulling describes tension.
Encouraging adjacent sections to slide describes shear.
Correct. Compression is the squeezing effect of forces on a material or component.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the force definitions in the load-path paragraph and match “squeezes” to the correct term.

questions.prompt: A frame shifts during a teacher-approved check. Why is adding extra material without tracing the load path weak reasoning?
options: Extra material always removes the forces from a structure
The extra material may add waste without addressing the joint, alignment or force route causing the movement
Only the surface appearance of a frame affects movement
A frame cannot experience more than one type of force

feedback.message: Material can carry or redirect forces, but it does not make forces disappear.
Correct. A useful change must respond to evidence about the actual load path and relationships.
Structural movement depends on connected members, joints, supports and forces, not surface appearance alone.
Different parts of a frame can experience compression, tension, bending, shear or torsion.

questions.help_prompt: Return to the warning that more material does not automatically repair the cause of a structural problem.

written_response.title: Trace a sideways movement through the structure
written_response.prompt: During a teacher-approved check, a frame looks neat but shifts sideways. Explain how a load path, at least two possible force effects, alignment and joint relationships could contribute. Then justify the evidence needed before one structural change is recommended.

scaffold.label: Trace the path
scaffold.prompt: Start with where the force enters, which connected parts may carry it and where it reaches support.

scaffold.label: Name force effects
scaffold.prompt: Explain how two relevant effects such as compression, tension, bending, shear or torsion could appear in the path.

scaffold.label: Compare causes
scaffold.prompt: Separate an alignment or joint observation from a conclusion about its cause.

scaffold.label: Justify evidence
scaffold.prompt: State what would need to be checked and teacher-approved before recommending one change.

success_cues: Describes a connected load path
Uses structural-force terms accurately
Distinguishes observation from possible cause
Avoids prescribing an unapproved construction change

section_checks.section_title: Check quality and record real evidence

questions.prompt: Which folio record is strongest evidence of a production decision?
options: An uncaptioned photo of the workbench
A checkpoint photo with a caption identifying the issue, decision and result
A copied theory paragraph
A statement saying ‘it was good’

feedback.message: Without context, the image does not show what was checked or decided.
Correct. The caption makes the evidence meaningful by linking observation, action and result.
Copied theory does not prove what happened in the student's production process.
The judgement is too vague to show a quality check or evidence.

questions.help_prompt: Choose evidence that records what was observed, what changed and why it mattered.

questions.prompt: Which set is most suitable for a teacher-approved frame checkpoint?
options: Colour, popularity and speed
Squareness, symmetry, joint quality and stability
Maximum power and competition rank
Number of photographs, page count and writing length

feedback.message: These features do not establish the structural readiness of the frame.
Correct. These observations can reveal alignment, construction and stability issues before later work.
A quality checkpoint is not a power competition and does not establish a test procedure.
Evidence quantity does not establish structural quality; the checkpoint needs relevant observations.

questions.help_prompt: Focus on observable structural qualities that affect later component alignment.

questions.prompt: Several individual parts match their planned sizes, but the assembled frame is out of alignment. What does this show?
options: Accurate individual parts automatically guarantee system quality
Alignment matters only after testing is complete
Quality also depends on relationships among parts, not only the accuracy of each part
The only useful response is to add more material

feedback.message: Correct individual parts can still be positioned or connected poorly as a system.
Alignment should be checked at planned production checkpoints before faults affect later work.
Correct. System quality includes how parts align, connect and remain stable together.
Extra material may add waste and does not establish or correct the actual cause.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the sentence explaining that accurate individual parts can still form a misaligned system.

questions.prompt: Which claim is still outside what a well-captioned production photograph can prove by itself?
options: A visible alignment issue existed at the checkpoint
A recorded adjustment changed the visible relationship between parts
The student was observed using the process safely and competently
The caption identifies why the photographed detail mattered

feedback.message: A clear photograph and caption can record a visible alignment issue.
Matched before-and-after evidence can show a visible change when the caption explains it honestly.
Correct. Safe practical competence requires teacher observation and local records; a photograph cannot establish it by itself.
A caption can explicitly state the evidence value of the photographed detail.

questions.help_prompt: Separate student-created visual evidence from teacher-controlled observation of safe practical performance.

written_response.title: Turn a checkpoint into meaningful evidence
written_response.prompt: Choose a real or teacher-provided production checkpoint. Explain what was observed, how it relates to system quality, what decision followed and what changed. Include a caption for one useful photograph or, if no image is available, describe the exact evidence a photograph would need to show.

scaffold.label: Observation
scaffold.prompt: Start with: “At the checkpoint, I observed ___.” Keep it specific and visible.

scaffold.label: Quality link
scaffold.prompt: Explain how the observation relates to alignment, stability, symmetry, joint quality or material efficiency.

scaffold.label: Decision and result
scaffold.prompt: Name the teacher-approved response and compare the later evidence with the earlier observation.

scaffold.label: Evidence limit
scaffold.prompt: State what the record shows and what it cannot prove about teacher-observed safe competence.

success_cues: Records a specific observation
Links evidence to a relevant quality relationship
Explains the decision and resulting evidence
Maintains the boundary between a folio record and teacher observation

scaffold.label: Structure
scaffold.prompt: Trace one possible load path and identify the types of force that could matter.

scaffold.label: Check
scaffold.prompt: Select two observable quality checks and explain what each could reveal.

scaffold.label: Record
scaffold.prompt: Write a photo caption or note that states observation, decision and next approved action.

success_cues: Explains a real process dependency
Uses load-path or structural-force language
Chooses observable quality evidence
Records evidence without claiming teacher-observed competence

theory_concepts.title: Quality depends on alignment and fit

questions.prompt: Why is a component-interaction chain more useful than a parts list?
options: It shows how an input or movement passes through connected components
It guarantees every design uses identical parts
It supplies an assembly recipe
It removes the need for testing

feedback.message: Correct. The chain explains relationships and helps trace the effect of a change.
Authorised designs may use different component arrangements.
A conceptual interaction chain does not prescribe a practical sequence.
Testing is still needed to check how the real system behaves.

questions.help_prompt: Look for the representation that explains what one component does to or with the next.

questions.prompt: A pivot develops unwanted movement. Why might this affect more than one component?
options: System components interact, so movement can change alignment, friction and energy transfer elsewhere
Every problem is caused by the base
The pivot is outside the system
One component can never influence another

feedback.message: Correct. A local issue can propagate through the interaction chain.
The base is one possible influence, but evidence is needed before naming a cause.
A pivot is a possible interacting component within the designed system.
Mutual influence is a defining feature of a system.

questions.help_prompt: Trace what the changed pivot position or movement could do to neighbouring parts.

questions.prompt: Which component-function statement is supported by the theory?
options: A pivot permits controlled rotation between related parts
The base creates all of the system's stored energy
A fastener decides the local testing rules
An energy store guarantees accurate and consistent results

feedback.message: Correct. A pivot provides a relationship that allows controlled rotation.
The base supports and locates components; it is not described as creating all stored energy.
Fasteners connect parts, while local test rules remain teacher-controlled.
An energy store supplies energy, but system quality still depends on alignment, fit, control and evidence.

questions.help_prompt: Return to the first paragraph and match each component with the function stated there.

questions.prompt: After the position of one component changes, which follow-up check uses systems thinking?
options: Assume the change affects only that component
Check neighbouring clearance, alignment, friction and the forces carried by the frame
Judge the result only by appearance
Skip testing because the parts list is unchanged

feedback.message: A position change can affect connected components and their interactions.
Correct. These checks trace likely downstream effects through the component chain.
Appearance alone cannot show whether the changed relationship works as intended.
An unchanged parts list does not mean the relationships or behaviour are unchanged.

questions.help_prompt: Follow the arrows in a system map from the changed component to the relationships around it.

written_response.title: Explain a component interaction chain
written_response.prompt: Create a written interaction chain for an approved Catapult design without giving assembly instructions. Explain how energy or movement passes through at least three connected component functions, then predict two downstream effects if the pivot position changes.

scaffold.label: Purpose and input
scaffold.prompt: Start with the intended system purpose and the input entering the interaction chain.

scaffold.label: Connected functions
scaffold.prompt: Use arrows in words: “___ affects ___, which then ___.” Name functions rather than prescribing a design.

scaffold.label: Predicted effects
scaffold.prompt: Predict how a pivot-position change could affect clearance, alignment, friction or frame forces.

scaffold.label: Evidence needed
scaffold.prompt: Identify the teacher-approved observations or checks needed before accepting either prediction.

success_cues: Explains interactions rather than listing parts
Uses at least three component functions accurately
Predicts more than one plausible downstream effect
Requests evidence instead of claiming an untested cause

section_checks.section_title: Quality depends on alignment and fit

questions.prompt: Which observation is most useful evidence of an alignment problem?
options: A moving part rubs consistently at the same point
The timber has a pleasant colour
The design is popular
The folio has many words

feedback.message: Correct. Repeated contact at one point can indicate misalignment or poor fit.
Colour does not establish component alignment.
Popularity is not technical evidence of fit or function.
Folio length does not establish the quality of the assembly.

questions.help_prompt: Choose an observation directly connected to position, clearance or contact between parts.

questions.prompt: Why can reducing friction have a trade-off?
options: Some friction may be needed for control or holding, while unwanted friction wastes energy and causes wear
All friction is always harmful
Friction occurs only when parts are misaligned
Friction can be removed by adding more energy

feedback.message: Correct. Designers distinguish useful friction from unwanted resistance.
Some friction is useful for grip, holding and control.
Friction can occur between aligned surfaces too; misalignment may increase unwanted contact but is not the only cause.
More stored energy does not remove the cause of friction and may create new demands.

questions.help_prompt: Consider where friction supports control and where it reduces useful motion.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes play from stiffness?
options: Play is useful friction, while stiffness is unwanted rubbing
Play and stiffness both mean a part is perfectly aligned
Play describes material colour, while stiffness describes surface finish
Play is unwanted free movement, while stiffness is resistance to changing shape

feedback.message: Play concerns unwanted movement; friction is resistance between contacting surfaces.
Neither term proves alignment, and excessive play can indicate a poor relationship.
Both terms describe mechanical behaviour rather than appearance.
Correct. The terms describe different behaviours that can both affect system quality.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the definitions in the second paragraph: one concerns free movement and the other shape change.

questions.prompt: Why can individually strong components still form an unreliable system?
options: Strength automatically removes friction
Reliability depends only on the number of fasteners
The parts stop interacting once they are assembled
Connections, alignment, fit and load transfer can still create weak or inconsistent relationships

feedback.message: Strong parts can still rub or resist movement if their relationship is poor.
Fastener quantity alone does not establish position, suitability, security or system behaviour.
Assembly creates the interactions that determine how the system behaves.
Correct. System quality depends on the relationships between parts as well as each part's properties.

questions.help_prompt: Think beyond the strength of one part and inspect what happens where components meet and transfer forces.

written_response.title: Judge an alignment–friction trade-off
written_response.prompt: A teacher-approved adjustment reduces unwanted rubbing but increases sideways movement. Explain why this is a system trade-off and decide whether the change should be accepted, reversed or retested using evidence about alignment, friction, play, stiffness and fit.

scaffold.label: Before and after
scaffold.prompt: State the original observation and the two changes in behaviour after the adjustment.

scaffold.label: System relationship
scaffold.prompt: Explain how reduced friction and increased play or misalignment can occur together.

scaffold.label: Evidence
scaffold.prompt: Identify at least two comparable observations needed to judge the trade-off under the same approved check.

scaffold.label: Decision
scaffold.prompt: Choose accept, reverse or retest and justify it against the confirmed function or criterion.

success_cues: Recognises improvement in one feature and decline in another
Uses alignment, friction, play, stiffness or fit accurately
Bases the decision on comparable evidence
Links the judgement to an authorised purpose rather than preference

questions.prompt: What is the strongest first response when a component no longer moves as expected at a teacher-approved check?
options: Add more elastic energy
Stop, inspect the interaction and record the evidence before one approved adjustment
Change several parts quickly
Ignore it until demonstration day

feedback.message: Adding energy does not identify the cause and can increase demands on the system.
Correct. The loop protects evidence and makes the effect of one change easier to judge.
Several changes hide which adjustment affected the result.
Delaying the check can embed the fault and weaken later evidence.

questions.help_prompt: Choose the response that preserves safety, identifies a likely cause and supports a fair comparison.

questions.prompt: Why is ‘more elastic energy is always better’ a misconception?
options: More stored energy can increase forces and expose alignment, stiffness or control problems
Elastic materials cannot store energy
System quality depends only on appearance
Energy has no relationship to component motion

feedback.message: Correct. A change in energy affects the whole interaction chain and must be judged against authorised criteria and controls.
Elastic deformation can store energy within the material's working range.
Quality also involves function, fit, evidence and response to the brief.
Energy transfer is what produces component motion in the system.

questions.help_prompt: Think about the extra demands increased energy can place on connected parts.

questions.prompt: Why should the same relevant check be repeated after one teacher-approved adjustment?
options: To guarantee that the result improves
To avoid recording the earlier problem
To create a fairer before-and-after comparison of the adjustment's effect
To allow several other features to change at the same time

feedback.message: An adjustment may improve, worsen or not change the result; the repeated check supplies evidence.
The earlier observation is needed as the comparison point.
Correct. Repeating the same check makes the evidence more useful for judging the single adjustment.
Other simultaneous changes would make the cause of any new result unclear.

questions.help_prompt: Ask what must stay comparable if you want to judge the effect of one change.

questions.prompt: An approved adjustment makes the result worse. What is the strongest evidence-led response?
options: Hide the result and keep the adjustment
Record the comparison, discuss the evidence with the teacher, then decide whether to reverse or retest
Immediately change several other components
Add more stored energy so the problem is less visible

feedback.message: Hiding a result removes evidence needed for a sound next decision.
Correct. A worse result is useful evidence when it is recorded and used to guide one approved next step.
Several changes would obscure which adjustment affects the behaviour.
More stored energy does not identify the cause and can increase demands elsewhere in the system.

questions.help_prompt: Use the full stop–check–adjust–record loop, including an honest comparison when the prediction is not supported.

written_response.prompt: Use a real or teacher-provided assembly observation to write a complete adjustment record. Separate what was observed from the possible cause, predict the effect of one teacher-approved change, compare the repeated check and justify the next decision.

scaffold.prompt: Use the evidence to justify keeping, reversing or retesting the change.

success_cues: Keeps observation and possible cause separate
Changes only one teacher-approved feature
Uses a comparable before-and-after check
Records an evidence-led next decision
