questions.prompt: Which is the strongest testable question for a teacher-controlled comparison?
options: Is my design awesome?
How does one approved design change affect the agreed measure when other conditions stay consistent?
Can I change everything and see what happens?
Which design looks fastest?

feedback.message: Personal approval is not a defined measure.
Correct. It identifies one change, a measure and the need for consistent conditions.
Changing everything prevents a clear cause-and-effect judgement.
Appearance does not provide performance evidence.

questions.help_prompt: Look for one changed variable, one agreed measure and controlled conditions.

questions.prompt: Who sets the projectile, test area, launch procedure and local controls for this project?
options: The website
Each student independently
The teacher through the approved local test procedure
Another course's instructions

feedback.message: These local testing details are deliberately absent from the website.
Students must not create their own unapproved testing procedure.
Correct. Testing occurs only under the teacher's approved local conditions.
Another course cannot authorise this class's procedure or controls.

questions.help_prompt: Distinguish scientific planning from authority for the physical test.

questions.prompt: Repeated results are grouped closely together but remain away from an agreed target. Which quality is strongest?
options: Accuracy, because the results are close to the target
Stability, because the frame must have stayed still
Consistency, because the repeated results are close to one another
Distance, because every grouped result travels far

feedback.message: The results are not described as close to the agreed target, so accuracy is not established.
The grouping alone does not establish what the supporting system did during testing.
Correct. Closely grouped repeated results indicate consistency even if they are not accurate.
No distance or high-result information is supplied.

questions.help_prompt: Separate closeness to a target from closeness among repeated results.

questions.prompt: In a teacher-approved comparison, one feature is deliberately changed and measurements respond. How should those variables be labelled?
options: The changed feature is independent and the measurements are dependent data
The changed feature is dependent and the measurements are controlled
Both are controlled variables
Both are independent variables

feedback.message: Correct. The independent variable is deliberately changed and the dependent data may respond.
The deliberately changed feature is the independent variable, not the dependent one.
A controlled variable is an important condition kept consistent, not the chosen change or resulting data.
Only the selected feature should be deliberately changed in a controlled comparison.

questions.help_prompt: Find the variable the investigator chooses to change, then identify what is observed or measured in response.

written_response.title: Frame a fair, teacher-controlled investigation
written_response.prompt: Draft a testable question for one teacher-confirmed Catapult feature and one agreed measure. Explain the independent variable, dependent data and controlled variables, then state which physical testing details remain set by the teacher.

scaffold.label: Question
scaffold.prompt: Use: “How does changing ___ affect ___ when ___ stays consistent?” Do not invent a project value.

scaffold.label: Variables
scaffold.prompt: Identify the one changed feature, the evidence that may respond and the important conditions to keep consistent.

scaffold.label: Measure
scaffold.prompt: Explain why the agreed measure answers the question, distinguishing distance, accuracy, consistency or stability.

scaffold.label: Authority boundary
scaffold.prompt: State that the teacher confirms the projectile, area, procedure, supervision and local controls.

success_cues: Names one changed feature and one relevant measure
Classifies variables accurately
Explains why the comparison could be meaningful
Does not invent or authorise physical test conditions

section_checks.section_title: Use repeated data, mean and range

questions.prompt: A generic practice dataset is 38, 42, 40 and 40 units. What is its mean?

feedback.message: Four is the number of values, not their mean.
Thirty-eight is the lowest result, not the mean.
Correct. The total is 160 units and 160 ÷ 4 = 40 units.
Forty-two is the highest result, not the mean.

questions.help_prompt: Add all results, then divide by the number of results.

questions.prompt: For the same practice dataset, what does the range of 4 units show?
options: The average result
The spread between the highest and lowest results
The number of controlled variables
The result every repeated trial should exactly match

feedback.message: The average is the mean, which is 40 units in this dataset.
Correct. Range is 42 − 38 = 4 units and gives a simple view of spread.
Controlled variables are recorded separately from the result range.
Real repeated results can vary; range describes that variation rather than setting a required result.

questions.help_prompt: Subtract the smallest result from the largest result and describe what that difference represents.

questions.prompt: One valid repeated result differs noticeably from the rest. What is the strongest response?
options: Delete it because it weakens the pattern
Record it as a possible anomaly and investigate what evidence could explain it
Replace it with the mean
Use only that result because it is memorable

feedback.message: Removing an inconvenient valid result can misrepresent the dataset.
Correct. An anomaly should be recorded and examined rather than hidden or accepted without question.
The mean summarises the set; it does not replace an individual valid result.
One unusual result cannot represent the full repeated pattern.

questions.help_prompt: Revisit the sentence explaining how to treat an anomaly honestly.

questions.prompt: Two practice datasets have the same mean, but Dataset A has the smaller range. What can be concluded from that information alone?
options: Dataset A is more consistent in this comparison
Dataset A is more accurate against every possible target
Dataset A proves the whole design is better
Dataset A contains more trials

feedback.message: Correct. A smaller range indicates less spread across the recorded results.
Accuracy needs an agreed target; equal means and different ranges do not establish it.
Range describes spread, not every criterion or system trade-off.
Range does not reveal how many trials are in each dataset.

questions.help_prompt: Use the role of range: it describes spread, while the mean describes the centre.

written_response.title: Interpret repeated evidence honestly
written_response.prompt: Use a teacher-provided or clearly labelled practice dataset of repeated results. Calculate or identify the mean and range, describe the pattern and any possible anomaly, then explain how confident you should be in one conclusion.

scaffold.label: Record and calculate
scaffold.prompt: Show the heading, confirmed unit, valid results, mean method and range method.

scaffold.label: Describe the pattern
scaffold.prompt: State what the centre and spread reveal without selecting only the best result.

scaffold.label: Investigate variation
scaffold.prompt: Identify any anomaly or variation and suggest evidence that could help explain it.

scaffold.label: Qualify the conclusion
scaffold.prompt: Write: “The evidence supports ___, but my confidence is limited by ___; further evidence should ___.”

success_cues: Uses mean and range for their correct purposes
Keeps all valid repeated results visible
Treats an anomaly as a question for investigation
Matches the strength of the conclusion to the available evidence

section_checks.section_title: Reason from evidence and redesign carefully

questions.prompt: Which statement follows claim–evidence–reasoning?
options: The change was better because I liked it
The adjusted system was more consistent; its repeated results had a smaller range, which indicates less variation under the same conditions
The highest result proves everything
The change worked, so no evidence is needed

feedback.message: Preference is not performance evidence.
Correct. It makes a claim, cites repeated data and explains why the evidence supports the claim.
One extreme result does not show a reliable pattern.
A claim needs evidence and reasoning to be defensible.

questions.help_prompt: Find the option containing a judgement, specific evidence and an explanation linking them.

questions.prompt: Why should redesign usually change one feature before retesting?
options: It makes the design look simpler
It supports a clearer link between the change and any new result
It guarantees improvement
It avoids teacher approval

feedback.message: Appearance is not the reason for controlled redesign.
Correct. A single change makes cause-and-effect reasoning more defensible.
A controlled change can make the result better, worse or unchanged.
Practical changes and retesting remain teacher-approved.

questions.help_prompt: Ask how the designer could tell which change caused the new result.

questions.prompt: After one redesign, the mean measured distance increases but the range of measured distances also becomes larger. What does the evidence show?
options: Every aspect of the design improved
The redesign must be accepted because the mean is the only useful measure
The mean measured distance increased while the results became less consistent; whether this is an improvement depends on the confirmed purpose
The results are invalid because two statistics changed

feedback.message: The larger range indicates increased variation, so the evidence does not show improvement in every aspect.
Range and relevant observations also matter when consistency or control is important.
Correct. The mean measured distance and range point to different effects that must be judged against the confirmed purpose.
Different changes in mean and range can reveal a real design trade-off.

questions.help_prompt: Interpret the mean as centre and the range as spread, then compare both with the intended purpose.

questions.prompt: Which before-and-after comparison provides the clearest evidence about one redesign feature?
options: Several features change and only the best new result is kept
The design changes but the measure and unit also change
One approved feature changes, relevant conditions stay the same and repeated results are compared
The new design is judged from appearance without testing

feedback.message: Several changes and selective reporting make cause and effect unclear.
Changing the measure or unit prevents a direct before-and-after comparison.
Correct. One change, consistent conditions and repeated evidence support a defensible comparison.
Appearance alone does not answer a testable performance question.

questions.help_prompt: Look for the comparison that changes one feature while keeping the evidence-gathering method comparable.

written_response.title: Make a redesign decision with CER
written_response.prompt: Use before-and-after evidence from one teacher-approved redesign or a supplied scenario. Write a claim–evidence–reasoning explanation, judge any trade-off, and recommend whether the change should be kept, reversed or retested.

scaffold.label: Claim
scaffold.prompt: Answer the test question with a focused judgement about the one changed feature.

scaffold.label: Evidence
scaffold.prompt: Select the relevant repeated pattern, mean, range and observations rather than one preferred result.

scaffold.label: Reasoning
scaffold.prompt: Explain the link using stability, alignment, friction, energy transfer or variation.

scaffold.label: Decision and limit
scaffold.prompt: Choose keep, reverse or retest, name the trade-off or limitation and identify useful further evidence.

success_cues: Keeps claim, evidence and reasoning distinct
Uses repeated before-and-after evidence
Acknowledges a relevant trade-off or limitation
Makes one justified and teacher-controlled next recommendation

capstone.title: Make a redesign decision from repeated evidence
capstone.prompt: Two teacher-controlled test sets are available: one before a design change and one after it. Decide whether the change should be kept, reversed or retested.

scaffold.label: Question
scaffold.prompt: State the changed variable, agreed measure and important controlled conditions.

scaffold.label: Calculate
scaffold.prompt: Compare the mean and range for the two result sets.

scaffold.label: Interpret
scaffold.prompt: Identify a pattern or anomaly and explain its effect on confidence.

scaffold.label: Decide
scaffold.prompt: Write a claim–evidence–reasoning judgement and one careful next step.

success_cues: Defines a fair comparison
Calculates and interprets mean and range
Does not rely on one best result
Makes a justified keep, reverse or retest decision

theory_concepts.title: Build a report around the design journey
Think across environmental, social and economic needs

section_checks.section_title: Build a report around the design journey

questions.prompt: Which report order creates the clearest engineering story?
options: Conclusion, title, unrelated theory, brief
Brief, design decision, production evidence, test method and results, discussion, sustainability, conclusion
Photographs only
A list of tools followed by a personal rating

feedback.message: This order hides the problem, evidence and reasoning that support the conclusion.
Correct. It follows the journey from the problem through decisions and evidence to a conclusion.
Images need captions and explanation to become engineering evidence.
A tool list and rating do not explain the design journey or test evidence.

questions.help_prompt: Choose the order that lets a reader follow problem, decision, action, evidence and judgement.

questions.prompt: Where should unexpected variation in test results be discussed?
options: Hide it so the report looks stronger
In the discussion, with possible causes and limits on the conclusion
Only in the title
Replace it with the best result

feedback.message: Omitting inconvenient evidence weakens the report's honesty and reasoning.
Correct. A discussion interprets patterns, anomalies, uncertainty and design implications.
A title identifies the report; it cannot analyse evidence.
Replacing repeated data with one result misrepresents performance.

questions.help_prompt: Think about which report section explains what the results mean and how certain the judgement is.

questions.prompt: Why does naming a limitation strengthen an engineering report?
options: It removes the need for a conclusion
It proves the design failed
It allows inconvenient results to be deleted
It shows how confident the conclusion should be and what further evidence may help

feedback.message: The conclusion is still needed to answer the original problem with the available evidence.
A limitation describes the evidence boundary; it does not automatically mean the design failed.
Honest reports retain relevant evidence, including inconvenient results.
Correct. A limitation makes the boundaries of the judgement visible and guides useful further investigation.

questions.help_prompt: Return to the second paragraph and ask what a limitation tells the reader about confidence.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best closes an engineering report?
options: A new claim that was not tested or discussed
A repeat of the brief with no judgement
A list of every photograph in the folio
An answer to the original problem supported by the strongest discussed evidence and a stated limit

feedback.message: A conclusion should not introduce an unsupported new claim.
Restating the problem does not explain what the evidence supports.
Evidence should be selected and interpreted, not merely listed.
Correct. The conclusion closes the journey by answering the original problem at an appropriate level of confidence.

questions.help_prompt: Choose the ending that returns to the original problem and uses evidence already developed in the report.

written_response.title: Build a connected report journey
written_response.prompt: Plan a short engineering report around one real design decision. Explain how the brief led to the decision, which production and test evidence matters, what the results mean and how the conclusion answers the original need without overstating certainty.

scaffold.label: Problem and decision
scaffold.prompt: State the authorised need or boundary, then identify the design decision being explained.

scaffold.label: Evidence trail
scaffold.prompt: Select one meaningful production record and one relevant test record; explain why each belongs.

scaffold.label: Discussion
scaffold.prompt: Interpret the result pattern, possible cause and one limitation rather than listing data.

scaffold.label: Conclusion
scaffold.prompt: Answer the original problem using the strongest evidence and state what further evidence would improve confidence.

success_cues: Follows the design journey in a logical order
Selects relevant production and test evidence
Interprets evidence rather than listing it
Concludes within the limits of the available evidence

questions.prompt: Which sentence is evidence rather than a claim?
options: Pine was the best possible material
The frame remained aligned at the recorded checkpoint
Therefore the design should be copied
Sustainability does not matter

feedback.message: ‘Best possible’ is a broad claim that would need comparison evidence.
Correct. It records an observable result that could support a later claim.
This is a recommendation, not the observation supporting it.
This is an unsupported judgement and conflicts with the report's required sustainability thinking.

questions.help_prompt: Evidence is the observation, measurement or record; a claim is the judgement made from it.

questions.prompt: What does the reasoning part of CER do?
options: Repeats the claim in longer words
Explains why the evidence supports the claim using relevant concepts
Adds another observation without linking it to the claim
Removes uncertainty from all results

feedback.message: Restating a claim does not connect it to the evidence.
Correct. Reasoning is the bridge between what was observed and what is concluded.
Another observation may strengthen the evidence, but reasoning must still explain its relevance to the claim.
Strong reasoning acknowledges limits rather than pretending uncertainty is absent.

questions.help_prompt: Look for the sentence that answers ‘how does this evidence support the judgement?’

questions.prompt: Which record is strongest evidence for the claim that an alignment adjustment improved component movement?
options: A before-and-after record from the same relevant check, with the adjustment and observed movement identified
A final photograph with no caption
A statement that the project looks better
A copied definition of alignment

feedback.message: Correct. The matched observations are relevant to the claim and make the change traceable.
Without context or a comparison, the image does not show the adjustment's effect.
Appearance and preference do not establish improved movement.
A definition explains the concept but does not show what happened in this project.

questions.help_prompt: Choose evidence that directly compares the claimed behaviour before and after the identified change.

questions.prompt: What should a report writer do when two relevant pieces of evidence point in different directions?
options: Hide the less convenient evidence
Acknowledge the conflict and examine variables, measurement limits or system interactions that may explain it
Choose the result that supports the preferred claim
State that evidence is no longer useful

feedback.message: Omitting relevant evidence weakens the report's honesty and credibility.
Correct. Careful reasoning explains uncertainty and identifies what further evidence may be needed.
Selecting only supportive results creates a biased judgement.
Conflicting evidence can reveal variation, limitations or a trade-off worth investigating.

questions.help_prompt: Return to the theory sentence explaining how credible reports handle conflicting evidence.

written_response.title: Write a qualified CER paragraph
written_response.prompt: Choose one real or teacher-provided project claim and the most relevant evidence record. Write a claim–evidence–reasoning paragraph that explains the engineering link, acknowledges any conflicting evidence or limitation, and avoids exaggerated certainty.

scaffold.label: Claim
scaffold.prompt: Write one focused judgement that answers a clear project question.

scaffold.label: Evidence
scaffold.prompt: Name the specific observation, measurement, drawing, photograph or production record that supports it.

scaffold.label: Reasoning
scaffold.prompt: Use a relevant material, structure, system, force or testing concept to explain why the evidence supports the claim.

scaffold.label: Qualification
scaffold.prompt: Add: “However, ___ limits this conclusion, so further evidence should ___.”

success_cues: Uses a focused and answerable claim
Selects specific relevant evidence
Explains the logical engineering link
Acknowledges uncertainty or conflicting evidence honestly

section_checks.section_title: Think across environmental, social and economic needs

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest sustainability judgement?
options: Pine is natural, so every use is automatically sustainable
A decision considers material efficiency, responsible sourcing, repair, waste, cost and effects on people
The cheapest option is always sustainable
Only end-of-life matters

feedback.message: A natural material can still involve sourcing, waste, processing and end-of-life impacts.
Correct. Sustainability involves connected environmental, social and economic considerations.
Cost matters, but a single economic factor cannot represent the whole judgement.
Life-cycle thinking includes sourcing, production, use, repair and end-of-life.

questions.help_prompt: Choose the judgement that considers more than one sustainability dimension and more than one life-cycle stage.

questions.prompt: Why is reducing unused offcut alone not proof that a design is sustainable?
options: Material efficiency is useful, but sourcing, durability, repair, process, people and end-of-life also matter
Waste never matters
Sustainability can only be judged by price
The authorised 2400 mm limit is a sustainability rating

feedback.message: Correct. Waste reduction is one useful piece of a wider evidence-based judgement.
Waste matters; it simply does not provide the whole sustainability picture.
Economic evidence is only one sustainability dimension.
The 2400 mm figure is an authorised material constraint, not a complete sustainability rating.

questions.help_prompt: Think across the whole material life cycle and the three sustainability dimensions.

questions.prompt: Which sequence takes a life-cycle view of a material decision?
options: Colour, popularity, competition rank and decoration
Price only
End of life without considering any earlier stage
Sourcing, production, use and repair, then end of life

feedback.message: These features do not trace the material through its life cycle.
Cost is one economic consideration, not a complete life-cycle view.
End of life matters, but earlier sourcing, production, use and repair also affect the judgement.
Correct. This follows the material from its source through use and later decisions.

questions.help_prompt: Trace the material from where it comes from to what may happen after its useful life.

questions.prompt: A redesign reduces offcut but takes more production time. What is the strongest sustainability response?
options: Compare the environmental gain with economic and social effects, using evidence before reaching a qualified judgement
Declare it sustainable because waste decreased
Reject it because time is the only factor that matters
Ignore both effects because sustainability cannot involve trade-offs

feedback.message: Correct. A defensible judgement considers interacting dimensions and names the evidence and trade-off.
Reduced waste is useful evidence, but one factor does not establish the whole judgement.
Time matters economically and socially, but it is not the only sustainability consideration.
Sustainability decisions often involve trade-offs that should be made visible.

questions.help_prompt: Look for the response that considers environmental, social and economic effects together.

written_response.title: Make a balanced sustainability judgement
written_response.prompt: Evaluate one real or supplied material or production decision from the Catapult project. Use environmental, social and economic evidence across relevant life-cycle stages, explain one trade-off and propose a realistic improvement without claiming the project is automatically sustainable.

scaffold.label: Decision and evidence
scaffold.prompt: State the decision and the available project or source evidence; avoid relying on “pine is natural” as proof.

scaffold.label: Three dimensions
scaffold.prompt: Explain one relevant environmental, one social and one economic effect.

scaffold.label: Life cycle and trade-off
scaffold.prompt: Connect the effects to sourcing, production, use or repair, and end of life, then identify one tension between them.

scaffold.label: Qualified judgement
scaffold.prompt: Judge the decision, name missing evidence and propose one realistic improvement.

success_cues: Uses evidence from more than one sustainability dimension
Applies life-cycle thinking
Explains a genuine trade-off
Makes a qualified judgement rather than a green claim

scaffold.label: Context
scaffold.prompt: State the brief need and the decision being judged.

scaffold.label: Evidence
scaffold.prompt: Select one production or test record that genuinely relates to the decision.

scaffold.label: Reason
scaffold.prompt: Explain the link using a material property, system interaction or production concept.

scaffold.label: Sustainability
scaffold.prompt: Judge one environmental, one social and one economic consideration, then state a realistic improvement.

success_cues: Follows the design journey rather than listing facts
Uses relevant project evidence
Connects claim and evidence with technical reasoning
Makes a balanced, qualified sustainability judgement

questions.prompt: What is the strongest purpose for a teacher-controlled demonstration?
options: To compete for maximum power
To communicate how the system functions and what the evidence shows
To create a new test procedure on the spot
To replace the folio

feedback.message: The course emphasises controlled communication and evidence, not maximum-power competition.
Correct. A demonstration connects function, evidence and design decisions for an audience.
The physical procedure remains teacher-set and is not improvised by students.
The folio preserves the design journey and evaluation beyond the live demonstration.

questions.help_prompt: Choose the purpose that helps an audience understand function and evidence under teacher control.

questions.prompt: Which demonstration statement is evidence-led?
options: Mine is the best
Across the recorded trials, the results varied by ___; this influenced our decision to ___
It worked once, so testing is finished
The audience should trust us

feedback.message: A ranking needs agreed criteria and evidence, not assertion.
Correct. It cites repeated evidence and connects it to a design decision without inventing a value.
One result does not establish consistency or quality.
Engineering communication should show the evidence rather than demand trust.

questions.help_prompt: Look for a statement with a result pattern and the decision it informed.

questions.prompt: The system behaves differently from the prediction during a teacher-controlled demonstration. What is the strongest response?
options: Describe the actual evidence, compare it with the prediction and identify the next question
Hide the result so the explanation sounds confident
Repeat the demonstration using student-invented conditions
Claim the unexpected result proves the design is a failure

feedback.message: Correct. A truthful comparison shows engineering thinking and can guide later investigation.
Hiding the result removes useful evidence and weakens the explanation.
Any physical retest remains under teacher-set conditions and supervision.
One unexpected result does not prove total failure; it should be interpreted with the wider evidence.

questions.help_prompt: Return to the paragraph explaining why a difference between prediction and result is still useful evidence.

questions.prompt: Which preparation best supports a clear engineering demonstration?
options: Aim for the most dramatic movement regardless of the brief
Prepare a ranking without agreed criteria
Plan what the audience should notice, which relationship explains it and which evidence will be recorded
Replace repeated evidence with one impressive result

feedback.message: Drama or maximum movement is not automatically the confirmed purpose.
A ranking requires authorised criteria and relevant evidence.
Correct. This preparation connects purpose, component relationships and visible evidence.
One result cannot show the consistency or pattern available from repeated evidence.

questions.help_prompt: Choose the preparation that helps an audience connect an observation to the design decision being explained.

written_response.title: Prepare an evidence-led demonstration explanation
written_response.prompt: Write the explanation you would give during a teacher-controlled demonstration. Communicate the intended function, one key component relationship, the repeated evidence the audience should notice and how you would respond if the result differed from the prediction.

scaffold.label: Purpose
scaffold.prompt: Start with: “The intended function of this system is ___ under the confirmed conditions.”

scaffold.label: Relationship
scaffold.prompt: Explain how two or more connected component functions contribute to the observed behaviour.

scaffold.label: Evidence
scaffold.prompt: Select a repeated pattern or quality observation and state what it does—and does not—show.

scaffold.label: Truthful response
scaffold.prompt: Compare prediction and result, then name a useful next question while keeping any retest teacher-controlled.

success_cues: Communicates function rather than competition
Explains a component relationship
Uses repeated or directly relevant evidence
Treats an unexpected result honestly and safely

questions.prompt: Which sequence produces a strong evaluation?
options: Preference–praise–finish
Criterion–evidence–judgement–improvement
Photo–caption–opinion–finish
Tool list–colour–competition–result

feedback.message: Praise and preference do not show how the result met the brief.
Correct. This loop makes the judgement traceable and leads to a realistic next step.
A photo and caption can supply evidence, but an unsupported opinion and no improvement do not complete the evaluation.
These items do not form an evidence-based evaluation process.

questions.help_prompt: Choose the sequence that begins with what success means and ends with a justified next step.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between product and process evaluation?
options: Product evaluation judges the result; process evaluation judges how decisions and production unfolded
They are identical
Process evaluation judges only appearance
Product evaluation ignores the brief and uses personal preference

feedback.message: Correct. Both use evidence, but they focus on different parts of the design journey.
They are connected but ask different questions about result and journey.
Process evaluation includes planning, problem-solving, changes, material use and production evidence.
Product evaluation should use authorised criteria and evidence rather than personal preference alone.

questions.help_prompt: Separate what was made from how the work and decisions progressed.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a personal-learning evaluation rather than a diary comment?
options: I liked the project because it was fun
My planning improved after the checkpoint record showed I had begun a dependent task too early; next time I will place that check in the sequence first
Today was a good day
I used many tools

feedback.message: Enjoyment can be mentioned, but it does not explain a change in knowledge, skill or decision-making.
Correct. It uses evidence of a learning change and identifies a realistic next action.
A diary comment does not connect learning to evidence or improvement.
A tool count does not show what was learned or how decisions changed.

questions.help_prompt: Look for a reflection that identifies evidence of changed knowledge or practice and a justified next step.

questions.prompt: Why is “add more power, material or time” a weak automatic improvement?
options: Those additions always reduce quality
Improvements should never change a design
An improvement should address the evidence and likely cause, while extra resources may create new system trade-offs
Appearance is the only criterion that matters

feedback.message: An addition is not automatically harmful, but its effect needs evidence and context.
A justified improvement can change a design when it responds to evidence and is approved.
Correct. A useful improvement responds to the cause and considers consequences elsewhere in the system.
Evaluation uses the confirmed brief and criteria, not appearance alone.

questions.help_prompt: Return to the evaluation paragraph and ask whether the proposed change responds to the evidence and wider system.

written_response.title: Evaluate the result, process and learning
written_response.prompt: Choose one teacher-confirmed criterion and build a complete evaluation. Judge the product with evidence, explain one process or learning change, then recommend an improvement that addresses a likely cause and predicts an effect on the wider system.

scaffold.label: Criterion and evidence
scaffold.prompt: Name the confirmed criterion and select the clearest relevant record.

scaffold.label: Product judgement
scaffold.prompt: Explain how fully the evidence supports the criterion and identify a limitation.

scaffold.label: Process and learning
scaffold.prompt: Describe one decision or skill change and the evidence that shows what you learned.

scaffold.label: Improvement
scaffold.prompt: Propose one realistic change, explain the likely cause it addresses and predict one wider system effect to check.

success_cues: Uses criterion–evidence–judgement–improvement
Separates product evidence from process and learning reflection
Acknowledges a limitation
Connects the improvement to a likely cause and system consequence

questions.prompt: What makes Brewarrina Aboriginal Fish Traps and the Budj Bim Cultural Landscape useful systems-thinking contexts?
options: They can be treated as Catapult design templates
They show connected relationships among landscape, water, people, knowledge and ongoing care
They prove all engineered systems have the same purpose
They can be explained without cultural authority

feedback.message: These living cultural systems must not be reduced to templates for an unrelated classroom project.
Correct. Systems thinking can recognise interconnected elements while preserving distinct purpose and cultural context.
Shared systems ideas do not erase different purposes, places or knowledge traditions.
Authoritative Aboriginal-led sources and teacher context are essential.

questions.help_prompt: Choose the explanation that recognises relationships without turning the cultural systems into a generic analogy.

questions.prompt: Which response best respects cultural authority?
options: Generalise one account to all Aboriginal peoples
Use Aboriginal-led authoritative sources, name the specific system and avoid unsupported local claims
Copy the booklet's detailed claims without verification
Rename a Catapult feature after a cultural system

feedback.message: Aboriginal peoples, places and knowledge systems are diverse and should not be generalised.
Correct. Specific, sourced and contextualised language preserves both accuracy and respect.
The booklet introduces the topics but is not authority for unverified cultural detail.
Borrowing a cultural name for an unrelated feature is inappropriate and misleading.

questions.help_prompt: Look for the choice that is specific about source authority and avoids appropriation or generalisation.

Only a Catapult diagram can explain the place
Physical features are the only source of cultural authority

feedback.message: The source explains that the dry-stone walls and holding ponds work with changing Barwon River flows.
Baiame’s Ngunnhu is a distinct continuing cultural system and must not be treated as a Catapult analogy.
Cultural authority comes from the named people and authoritative sources, not physical features alone.

questions.prompt: Which account of Budj Bim Cultural Landscape is best aligned with the named authoritative sources?

It is an abandoned historical structure with no continuing cultural relationship
It connects volcanic landscape, waterways, channels, weirs and dams with kooyang, Gunditjmara knowledge, custodianship and care for Country
It matters only because of its World Heritage listing

feedback.message: Budj Bim is a distinct living cultural landscape, not a generic design template.
The sources describe a continuing Gunditjmara cultural landscape and living relationship with Country.

Using the named authoritative source on this page, explain the connected relationships the source supports, identify the people and continuing responsibilities, and justify why the system must remain distinct from the Catapult project.

Keeps people, Country, knowledge and physical relationships connected
Recognises continuing custodianship or responsibility
Avoids ranking, appropriation and false equivalence

Separates product and process evaluation
Proposes a realistic improvement

applied_learning_activity.title: Evidence-led demonstration and evaluation card
applied_learning_activity.purpose: Practise selecting evidence for a calm explanation and writing an evaluation that respects connected Aboriginal engineering contexts.
applied_learning_activity.lesson_placement: After evaluation and connected systems, before the module capstone
ordered_steps: Select one project claim and match it to the strongest available evidence type.
Write a three-sentence demonstration explanation with no performance ranking.
Complete one product and one process criterion–evidence–judgement–improvement loop.
Read a teacher-provided Aboriginal-led source extract and identify the interacting system elements it names.
Write one sentence explaining why the cultural system remains distinct from the Catapult project.
applied_learning_activity.evidence_to_save: Demonstration note, two evaluation loops and respectful systems-context statement, saved as formative practice.
applied_learning_activity.extension: Compare how maintenance and feedback sustain two unrelated systems while explicitly preserving their different purposes and cultural contexts.
applied_learning_activity.support: Use: ‘The evidence shows ___. Against the criterion, I judge ___. A realistic improvement is ___.’
applied_learning_activity.printable_option: Demonstration card, two evaluation loops and source-context note.

folio_connection.prompt: Use your strongest project evidence to complete the final product, process and personal-learning evaluation; keep cultural systems learning in the module response rather than claiming it as Catapult design evidence.
folio_connection.relationship: The activity prepares the final explanation; the folio stores only the student's project evaluation and selected evidence.

top_level_activity_bank.title: System chain sorter
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Rebuild the Catapult system from concept cards and explain why a set of parts is not automatically a system.
steps: Sort concept cards into input, process, output or feedback.
Order a neutral component chain from energy input to observable output.
Choose two neighbouring components and explain their interaction.
Predict one downstream effect if a component becomes misaligned.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Completed sort and two interaction explanations, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Reveal category feedback one card at a time, then compare the explanation with the interaction-chain success cues.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Start with what enters, what changes, what can be observed and what information returns to the designer.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Add a second feedback path and explain the decision it could influence.
top_level_activity_bank.printable_option: Cut-and-sort cards plus a four-column system map.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Criteria clinic
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Distinguish authorised constraints from useful criteria and repair vague evaluation statements.
steps: Sort eight statements into criterion, constraint, evidence or unsupported claim.
Explain why the 2400 mm planned-pine limit is a constraint.
Rewrite ‘works well’ as an observable criterion without inventing a threshold.
Match one evidence type to the rewritten criterion.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Sort result, repaired criterion and evidence match, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Feedback names the role of each statement and checks whether the rewrite is observable without adding an unauthorised value.
top_level_activity_bank.support: A constraint limits the design; a criterion describes what could be judged; evidence is what was observed or measured.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Write a criterion–evidence–judgement–improvement loop for the repaired criterion.
top_level_activity_bank.printable_option: Statement cards and a four-category answer table.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Tool function and stop–ask triage
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Connect a workshop need to a tool function while recognising when authority or information is missing.
steps: Match non-operational scenarios to measuring/marking, holding, cutting, shaping, drilling or joining.
Identify the material property that matters in two scenarios.
Mark each scenario proceed-after-demonstration, stop-and-ask or not-authorised-from-source.
Justify one decision using hazard, control and authority language.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Function matches and one justified triage decision, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Feedback explains function and authority without naming an operating procedure.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Ask: what function is needed, what material is involved, and what must the teacher confirm?
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Explain why a pictured tool is not automatically approved for use.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Lever moment reasoning lab
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Apply moment = force × perpendicular distance and explain the design trade-off in words.
steps: Label effort, pivot, load, effort arm and load arm on a generic lever diagram.
Calculate moments for three supplied non-project examples with units.
Identify which example is balanced and justify the decision.
Explain one trade-off created by increasing an arm length.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Label set, calculations and trade-off explanation, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Show calculation feedback after submission and require the written explanation to name force, distance and consequence.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Multiply force by perpendicular distance from the pivot and compare moments on opposite sides.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Create a new balanced numerical example that is clearly labelled as theory, not a project dimension.
top_level_activity_bank.printable_option: Generic lever diagrams and calculation table.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Energy and Newton misconception clinic
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Correct common errors about conservation of energy and Newton's laws using Catapult-linked concepts.
steps: Sort eight statements into defensible or misconception.
Repair one statement that says energy disappears.
Assign a first-, second- or third-law label to three conceptual observations.
Explain why a third-law pair acts on different objects.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Corrected statements and one law explanation, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Each statement receives concept-specific feedback; no answer is shown before the student chooses.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Track energy destinations and identify the object receiving each force.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Write one observation that could be explained by two concepts and distinguish their roles.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Drawing and cutting-list audit
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Check whether a generic design communication package is consistent, complete and ready for teacher approval.
steps: Compare part labels across generic front, top and side views.
Locate three conflicts between views and the generic cutting list.
Calculate quantity totals and the overall planned length.
Compare the total with the authorised 2400 mm limit.
Write a readiness note naming kerf and stock notation as teacher-confirmation points.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Conflict log, arithmetic and readiness note, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Feedback checks each conflict and calculation while stating that practice values are not Catapult dimensions.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Check one part at a time: label, dimension, quantity, total and agreement across records.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Write a revision note showing which records would need updating after one generic dimension changes.
top_level_activity_bank.printable_option: Generic three-view sheet and cutting-list audit table.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Load-path labeller
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Trace forces through a conceptual frame and explain how triangulation can resist shape change.
steps: Label force entry, members, joints, supports and ground reaction on a conceptual frame.
Classify five member descriptions as tension, compression, bending, shear or torsion.
Compare an unbraced rectangle and a triangulated frame.
Write one quality checkpoint that could reveal a broken load path.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Labelled path, classifications and checkpoint explanation, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Feedback explains the force route and allows keyboard selection instead of drag-and-drop.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Follow the force from where it enters until it reaches a supporting surface.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Describe how one weak joint could change forces in neighbouring members.
top_level_activity_bank.printable_option: Conceptual frame diagram and force-classification table.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Quality fault evidence matrix
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Separate observations from causes and choose evidence that could distinguish competing explanations.
steps: Read four quality observations involving alignment, friction, play, stiffness or stability.
For each, list two possible causes without selecting one too early.
Choose the evidence that would distinguish the causes.
Write one stop–check–adjust–record plan with a single teacher-approved change.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Cause/evidence matrix and one adjustment record, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Feedback rewards cautious causal reasoning and rejects multiple simultaneous changes.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Use ‘observed’, ‘possible cause’, ‘evidence needed’ and ‘one approved change’ as separate columns.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Add a system-chain consequence for each possible cause.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Repeated-data detective
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Use mean, range and pattern evidence instead of selecting one best result.
steps: Check the headings and units of two supplied practice data tables.
Calculate mean and range for each set.
Identify one pattern and one possible anomaly.
Choose keep, reverse or retest and justify it with CER.
Name one limitation of the practice dataset.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Calculations, anomaly note, CER decision and limitation, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Calculation feedback shows the method after submission; reasoning feedback checks whether the decision uses repeated evidence.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Mean describes centre; range describes spread; neither replaces attention to the full pattern.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Explain how an outlier could change the mean and what further evidence would help.
top_level_activity_bank.printable_option: Two data tables and CER decision frame.

top_level_activity_bank.title: CER paragraph repair shop
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Turn unsupported project statements into concise claim–evidence–reasoning explanations.
steps: Sequence mixed claim, evidence and reasoning sentences.
Identify what is missing from two weak paragraphs.
Repair one paragraph using a supplied evidence record.
Use a success-cue checklist to review the revised paragraph.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: One repaired CER paragraph and self-check, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Feedback identifies the function of each sentence and checks the logical bridge between evidence and claim.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Ask: what do I judge, what did I observe, and why does that observation support the judgement?
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Add a qualification that acknowledges a limitation without abandoning the conclusion.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Sustainability life-cycle sorter
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Build a balanced sustainability judgement from sourcing through end-of-life.
steps: Place twelve decision cards under sourcing, production, use/repair or end-of-life.
Tag each card environmental, social, economic or connected.
Identify one trade-off between two dimensions.
Improve the unsupported claim ‘pine is sustainable because it is natural’.
Write one realistic material-efficiency action within the authorised brief.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Life-cycle sort, trade-off and qualified sustainability judgement, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Feedback accepts connected classifications when the student explains the relationship and rejects single-factor certainty.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Consider where the material came from, how it is used, how long it lasts, who is affected and what happens later.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Compare repair and replacement using evidence needed, not assumed conclusions.

top_level_activity_bank.title: Authority, context and connected-systems inquiry
top_level_activity_bank.mechanic: source evaluation and contextual systems mapping
top_level_activity_bank.purpose: Use teacher-provided Aboriginal-led sources to recognise connected engineering relationships without appropriation or false equivalence.
steps: Read the authoritative source extracts embedded by the teacher or integrator, then check each for named authority, specific place/system and publication context.
Identify relationships among landscape, water, people, knowledge and maintenance that the source itself supports.
Separate source-supported statements from unsupported generalisations.
Write why the named cultural system must not be treated as a Catapult template or generic analogy.
Record one respectful question that would require further teacher or community context.
top_level_activity_bank.evidence_to_save: Source check, connected-system map and contextual statement, saved as formative practice.
top_level_activity_bank.feedback: Feedback checks provenance, specificity and respect; it does not quiz cultural detail or expose unsupported claims as facts.
top_level_activity_bank.support: Name the source and the specific system; write only what that source supports; preserve distinct purpose and cultural authority.
top_level_activity_bank.extension: Compare two authoritative accounts of the same named system and note how their purposes or audiences differ.

orientation.what_it_is: A calm record of the design decisions, project process, testing evidence and evaluation that best explain your Catapult project.
orientation.what_it_is_not: It is not a copy of every theory answer or quiz. Website records do not prove submission, teacher observation, safe-tool competence or a formal grade.
orientation.first_action: Start by writing the need and confirmed brief in your own words. The page then shows the next unfinished stage.
orientation.save_message: Your writing and optional images save on this browser as you work. Use Backup before changing device or clearing browser data.
orientation.drawing_message: No drawing is required in the website. Complete any paper drawing activities your teacher assigns in the source booklet, then optionally add a clear image with a caption.

storage_and_recovery.autosave: Save changed text after a short pause and show the last successful local save time; save image metadata immediately after validation.
storage_and_recovery.migration: Preserve compatible version-1 records. Future versions must migrate a copy before replacing the active record.
storage_and_recovery.reset: Reset affects only Catapult folio keys, requires the user to type RESET, and offers a backup first.
storage_and_recovery.backup: Download an editable, self-contained JSON backup with course ID, schema version, stage prompts, text, captions and the optional images currently stored for this folio.
storage_and_recovery.restore: Validate JSON, course ID, schema version, field types and image records before previewing the restore. Reject a wrong-course file; never merge silently.
storage_and_recovery.submission_export: Create a separate, read-only HTML evidence export with stage context, responses, captions and included images. Label it ‘Student-created evidence export — not proof of submission’.
storage_and_recovery.print: Print all completed stage evidence in readable order with prompt context, captions and available images; hide editing controls and retain the formative/submission boundary.
storage_and_recovery.privacy: Text and images remain on this browser unless the student deliberately downloads a backup/export or follows a separate teacher-confirmed submission process.

image_policy.validation_message: Choose a JPG, PNG or WebP image no larger than 5 MB. The image stays in this browser unless you export it.
image_policy.processing: Create a browser-local display copy, preserve the student's caption, and never upload automatically.
image_policy.evidence_rule: An image is useful only when its caption explains the decision, process, result or quality evidence it shows. Images are optional and are not a quota.

progress_model.rule: Derive progress from meaningful saved content, never from a mark or percentage score.
progress_model.next_action: Offer one next incomplete stage or one incomplete field within the current stage.

stages.title: Brief and criteria
stages.action: Explain the authorised need, constraints and confirmed success criteria in your own words.
stages.why: A clear brief gives every later decision something reliable to respond to.
stages.evidence: A concise need statement, the confirmed material/folio constraints, and testable criteria supplied or approved by the teacher.
stages.prompt: What must your Catapult project achieve, what confirmed boundaries apply, and what evidence could show success?

response_controls.label: Criteria status
options: Teacher to confirm
Confirmed by teacher

stages.caption: Not applicable unless an optional source image is added later.
support: The source confirms a timber Catapult, practical and folio, listed materials and a maximum of 2400 mm of planned pine lengths.
Do not add a projectile, performance threshold, launch condition or cross-section that has not been confirmed.
Sentence starter: ‘The project needs a solution that ___. A confirmed constraint is ___. Success could be judged by ___.’
stages.assessment_relationship: Selected folio evidence only; the website does not set formal criteria, marks, dates or a submission route.

stages.title: Research that informs the design
stages.action: Record only research findings that help explain a material, system or design decision.
stages.why: Useful research changes or strengthens a decision; copied facts do not show design thinking.
stages.evidence: At least one source-aware finding about pine, elastic behaviour, an engineered system or a lever relationship, plus its relevance to the project.
stages.prompt: Which reliable finding affected your thinking, where did it come from, and how could it influence a design decision?

response_controls.label: Context note if using Aboriginal engineering learning

stages.caption: If an optional image is added, explain what information it supports and identify its source; do not upload an image without permission.
support: Prefer authoritative government, museum, university, technical or Aboriginal-led sources suited to the claim.
The source booklet introduces woomera, Brewarrina and Budj Bim topics but is not authority for detailed cultural claims.
Sentence starter: ‘According to ___, ___. This matters to my decision because ___.’
stages.assessment_relationship: Research evidence selected by the student; no automatic mark or source-count threshold is created by the website.

stages.title: Different ideas
stages.action: Type four genuinely different idea summaries and compare their likely strengths, limits and questions.
stages.why: Exploring alternatives makes the chosen direction easier to justify and can prevent early commitment to a weak idea.
stages.evidence: Four typed idea summaries and a brief PMI comparison. Paper sketches from the booklet may be added as optional images.
stages.prompt: How does each idea arrange the system differently, and what must be checked before one is selected?

response_controls.label: Optional images of teacher-assigned paper sketches

stages.caption: State which idea the sketch shows and what design relationship it communicates.
support: No drawing is required in the website; use typing for every required online response.
Complete source-booklet drawings on paper when your teacher directs you.
Make the idea summaries different in system arrangement or interaction, not merely colour.
stages.assessment_relationship: Design-development evidence; optional images do not create a drawing quota or prove teacher approval.

stages.title: Chosen design
stages.action: Justify the selected idea and show that its drawing information and cutting list agree before production.
stages.why: A buildable design must communicate the same decision consistently across words, views, labels and material planning.
stages.evidence: A typed selection justification, consistency check, planned-pine arithmetic and teacher-confirmation state; optional images of paper drawings and cutting list.
stages.prompt: Why is this idea the strongest response to the brief, and what evidence shows that the design records agree?

response_controls.label: Drawing and list consistency
items: Planned pine total is no more than 2400 mm

response_controls.label: Optional images of my paper design records

stages.caption: Identify the view or list shown and explain what has been cross-checked; do not claim approval unless the teacher has provided it.
support: No drawing is required in the website. The source booklet separately asks for a preferred drawing, orthographic views and a cutting list.
The 2400 mm figure is a maximum planned-pine allowance, not a target.
Kerf and the ambiguous ‘10mm² Pine’ stock wording remain Teacher to confirm.
stages.assessment_relationship: Planning evidence only; the website does not approve dimensions, cutting or production readiness.

stages.title: Production planning
stages.action: Record a teacher-approved sequence of tasks, dependencies, checkpoints and required readiness evidence.
stages.why: A planned sequence protects time, materials and quality by placing decisions before dependent work.
stages.evidence: A typed production-plan table showing task purpose, dependency, tool function, teacher approval and checkpoint; no universal build recipe.
stages.prompt: What needs to happen, what does each task depend on, and where must you stop for a teacher-approved check?

response_controls.label: Plan state
options: Draft — Teacher to confirm
Teacher-approved for the next stage

stages.caption: If an optional plan image is added, explain which dependency or checkpoint it supports.
support: Name tool functions unless your teacher has confirmed the actual local tool and process.
OnGuard modules, machine permissions, local risk controls, PPE and Work Method Statement format remain teacher-controlled.
A production plan prepares decisions; it is not evidence that a student has been observed using a tool safely.
stages.assessment_relationship: Planning record only; safe use and readiness require teacher-controlled records outside automated folio judgement.

stages.title: Build checkpoints
stages.action: Capture a small number of meaningful checkpoints that explain progress, a problem, a decision or a quality improvement.
stages.why: Selected evidence makes the production story credible without turning the folio into a photo dump.
stages.evidence: Repeatable typed checkpoint cards with optional project images, each linking observation, decision, approved action and result.
stages.prompt: What did you observe at this checkpoint, what decision followed, and how did it affect the next stage?
stages.caption: Explain what the image proves about progress, quality, a problem or a change; an uncaptioned image is incomplete evidence.
support: Useful checks may include squareness, symmetry, joint quality, stability, alignment, fit, friction, play, stiffness or material use when approved by the teacher.
Do not write that the website has verified safe tool use or practical competence.
Sentence starter: ‘I observed ___. This mattered because ___. After teacher approval, I ___. The result was ___.’
stages.assessment_relationship: Student-created process evidence; teacher-observed practical evidence remains separate and is not inferred from a photo or typed claim.

stages.title: Testing and redesign
stages.action: Record the teacher-controlled test question, repeated results, pattern and one justified redesign decision.
stages.why: Repeated evidence makes a redesign decision more defensible than one memorable result.
stages.evidence: A test record with approved question and measure, repeated data, mean/range where suitable, pattern/anomaly note and controlled redesign decision.
stages.prompt: What does your repeated evidence show, how certain is the pattern, and what one change should be kept, reversed or retested?

response_controls.label: Optional teacher-authorised test or redesign evidence

stages.caption: Describe the test or changed feature shown and what the evidence adds; do not include unsafe, identifying or unauthorised images.
support: The teacher sets the projectile, area, procedure, controls, supervision and any thresholds; the website supplies none of these.
Use the full repeated pattern, not only the best result.
Change one approved feature, predict the effect and compare under the same teacher-set conditions.
stages.assessment_relationship: Student test and redesign evidence only; physical testing authority and teacher observation remain separate.

stages.title: Evaluation
stages.action: Judge the product, process and personal learning against the authorised brief and evidence, then propose a realistic improvement.
stages.why: Evaluation closes the design loop by turning evidence into a judgement and a useful next step.
stages.evidence: Environmental, personal/process and product evaluation using criterion–evidence–judgement–improvement, plus one final evidence selection.
stages.prompt: What worked, what did not, what evidence supports each judgement, and what would you improve next time?

response_controls.label: One realistic improvement and the evidence needed to test it

stages.caption: State what the final evidence shows against the brief or confirmed criterion; avoid ‘it was good’ without evidence.
support: Use criterion–evidence–judgement–improvement for each evaluation focus.

A balanced sustainability judgement can consider material efficiency, sourcing, durability, repair, process choices, people, cost and end-of-life without claiming the project is automatically ‘green’.
Sentence starter: ‘Against the criterion ____, the evidence shows ____. I judge ____. Next time I would ____ because ____.’
stages.assessment_relationship: Final student reflection and selected project evidence; the website does not assign a mark, record submission or replace teacher judgement.
